Lunar New Year foods.Dumplings: Dumplings are said to resemble ancient gold ingots, so eating them at the Lunar New Year is thought to invite wealth.
Lunar New Year foods.Spring rolls: Spring rolls are named for the spring season, and their golden color is meant to resemble gold bars and prosperity.
Lunar New Year foods.Nian gao: Nian gao is a sticky rice cake whose name sounds like 'higher year', so eating it is a wish for growth and progress.
Lunar New Year foods.Tangyuan: Tangyuan, sweet rice balls in soup, have a round shape and a name that echoes reunion, so they fit the holiday and family togetherness.
Lunar New Year foods.Longevity noodles: Longevity noodles are very long and are eaten uncut, since breaking them is thought to shorten your life.
Lunar New Year foods.Steamed fish: Fish is served on the Lunar New Year because the word for fish sounds like the word for surplus.
Lunar New Year foods.Mandarin oranges: Mandarin oranges are given as gifts at the Lunar New Year because their name sounds like luck and their gold color suggests wealth.
Lunar New Year foods.Tteokguk: Tteokguk, a Korean rice cake soup, is eaten on Seollal, and tradition says eating it makes you a year older.
Lunar New Year foods.Bánh chưng: Bánh chưng is a square sticky rice cake wrapped in leaves for Tết, and it is cooked for around ten hours.
Lunar New Year foods.Mooncake: Mooncakes belong to the Mid-Autumn Festival rather than the Lunar New Year, though both are major Chinese holidays.
Lunar New Year foods.Zongzi: Zongzi are tied to the Dragon Boat Festival in early summer, not to the Lunar New Year.
Lunar New Year foods.Hot cross bun: Hot cross buns are English Easter pastries, so they don't belong to the Lunar New Year.
Lunar New Year foods.Panettone: Panettone is the Italian Christmas cake from Milan, not a Lunar New Year food.
Lunar New Year foods.Pumpkin pie: Pumpkin pie is a North American Thanksgiving dessert, and it has no part in the Lunar New Year feast.
Lunar New Year foods.Candy corn: Candy corn is for Halloween, and it appears in October, not in Lunar New Year celebrations.
Lunar New Year foods.Latkes: Latkes are Hanukkah potato pancakes, a Jewish festival tradition and not a Lunar New Year food.
Lunar New Year foods.Hamantaschen: Hamantaschen are triangular Purim cookies, a Jewish holiday treat, and not part of the Lunar New Year.
Lunar New Year foods.Easter egg: Easter eggs belong to a spring Christian holiday, not to the Lunar New Year.
Lunar New Year foods.Gingerbread: Gingerbread is a Christmas favorite, with houses and cookies, and not a Lunar New Year food.
Lunar New Year foods.Matzo: Matzo is Passover's unleavened bread, which has no role in Lunar New Year feasts.
Lunar New Year foods.Mince pie: Mince pies are a British Christmas treat, and not a Lunar New Year food.
Lunar New Year foods.Pączki: Pączki are Polish doughnuts for Fat Thursday, which is not a Lunar New Year food.
Lunar New Year foods.Stollen: Stollen is a German Christmas fruit loaf, and not served at Lunar New Year.
Lunar New Year foods.Candy cane: Candy canes are Christmas decorations and treats, and don't belong to Lunar New Year.

Famous TV cooks and chefs.Gordon Ramsay: The Scottish-born chef is known for fiery shows like Hell's Kitchen and has earned multiple Michelin stars at his restaurants.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Jamie Oliver: The 'Naked Chef' rose to fame in the late 1990s and later campaigned to improve British school meals.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Julia Child: Her 1961 book Mastering the Art of French Cooking and TV show The French Chef taught America to cook French food.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Anthony Bourdain: The chef turned author and travel host of Parts Unknown, whose memoir Kitchen Confidential exposed restaurant life.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Nigella Lawson: The British food writer and TV cook, whose sensual, comfort-food style made her a household name, is the daughter of a Chancellor of the Exchequer.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Wolfgang Puck: Austrian-born, he pioneered California cuisine at Spago and also caters the Oscars' Governors Ball.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Emeril Lagasse: His catchphrase 'Bam!' and Louisiana-style cooking made him a star of the early Food Network.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Bobby Flay: A grill master who made his name with 'Beat Bobby Flay' on the Food Network, challenging other chefs.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Guy Fieri: With frosted spiky hair and Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives, this chef became Food Network's most recognizable face.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Ina Garten: The 'Barefoot Contessa' was once a White House nuclear policy analyst before she bought a Hamptons specialty food store.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Heston Blumenthal: The British chef's restaurant The Fat Duck is known for molecular gastronomy, with dishes like snail porridge.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Marco Pierre White: Often called the first celebrity chef, he became the youngest chef to win three Michelin stars, and mentored Gordon Ramsay.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Massimo Bottura: The Italian chef behind Osteria Francescana became famous on Netflix's Chef's Table and founded a food-waste charity.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Simon Cowell: A British TV judge of Pop Idol and The X Factor, not a chef.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Gordon Brown: A trap with Ramsay's first name: the former UK Prime Minister, not a chef.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Jamie Foxx: An Oscar-winning actor and singer for the film Ray, not a TV chef like Jamie Oliver.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Julia Roberts: The Pretty Woman star shares a first name with Julia Child, who she doesn't resemble; she's an actress.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Anthony Hopkins: The Welsh actor best known for Hannibal Lecter, who cooks in films but isn't a TV chef.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Guy Ritchie: A British film director known for Snatch, not a cook like Guy Fieri.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Bobby Moore: England's captain who lifted the 1966 World Cup, not a chef like Bobby Flay.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Wolfgang Mozart: The composer's first name matches Wolfgang Puck, but he was an 18th-century composer.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Jamie Lee Curtis: The actress from Halloween and Everything Everywhere All at Once shares only a name with Jamie Oliver.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Emma Watson: Best known as Hermione in the Harry Potter films, and she is not a TV cook.
Famous TV cooks and chefs.Mario Andretti: An Italian-American racing champion who won the Indy 500 and Formula One title, not Mario Batali the chef.

Served at a British afternoon tea.Scones: Split and eaten with jam and cream. Whether jam or cream goes first is a famous rivalry between Devon and Cornwall.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Clotted cream: A thick yellow cream made by slowly heating full-fat milk and skimming the crust, which is a specialty of Devon and Cornwall.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Cucumber sandwiches: Thin cucumber slices on crustless white bread, which became a symbol of Victorian refinement. Cucumbers were then a luxury in winter.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Jam: Jam spread on scones is a tea essential. Strawberry is the classic choice.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Earl Grey: A black tea scented with bergamot orange oil. Legend ties it to Prime Minister Earl Grey in the 1830s.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Victoria sponge: Named for Queen Victoria, who enjoyed a slice with her tea. It is jam and cream between two light sponge layers.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Finger sandwiches: Small crustless sandwiches with fillings like egg or smoked salmon. They are cut into 'fingers' so they can be eaten politely in a few bites.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Lemon curd: A tangy spread of lemon, sugar, eggs and butter. It often goes on scones and is a classic English preserve.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Petit fours: The name is French for 'small oven', and these bite-size cakes were once baked in the cooling oven after the main baking.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Darjeeling: Often called the 'champagne of teas', a delicate black tea from the Himalayan foothills of India, with muscatel notes.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Nachos: They came from Mexico in the 1940s, named after their inventor Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya, and are far from tea-table fare.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Pizza: Pizza is Italian street food, and a hot, cheesy meal doesn't fit the delicate afternoon tea.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Burrito: A large hearty Mexican wrap. It's far too filling for the dainty bites of afternoon tea.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Hot dog: A sausage in a bun is ballpark fare. Afternoon tea has small bites, not hot dogs.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Ramen: A Japanese noodle soup that is a hearty meal in itself, nothing like tea's finger food.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Chicken wings: Buffalo wings were created in Buffalo, New York in 1964. They are messy, spicy pub food, not tea fare.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Fries: Fries belong with fish and chips, but tea sandwiches and pastries are the tea table's fare.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Tacos: Tacos are casual Mexican street food. They're not served at a refined British tea.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Beer: Tea is a refined mid-afternoon ritual with, of course, tea. Beer belongs in the pub, not on the tea table.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Popcorn: A snack for the cinema, not the tea table, even though corn has been popped for thousands of years.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Pho: A Vietnamese noodle soup with a long-simmered broth. It is a full meal, far from a light tea.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Corn dog: A fairground food of a hot dog dipped in cornmeal batter and fried on a stick, and not suitable for fine tea.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Kebab: Grilled skewered meat from the Middle East and beyond. It is a substantial meal, not a dainty tea item.
Served at a British afternoon tea.Curry: Britain loves curry, and chicken tikka masala is sometimes called a national dish, but it's not a tea-time food.

Animals with a shell.Turtle: A turtle's shell is part of its skeleton, fused to the ribs and spine, so it can't leave it.
Animals with a shell.Tortoise: Tortoises are land turtles, and some, such as Galapagos giants, live for well over a century.
Animals with a shell.Snail: A snail's shell grows with it in a spiral and is made from calcium carbonate, which the snail secretes.
Animals with a shell.Crab: Crabs outgrow their shell, so they molt it, and during that time they're soft and vulnerable.
Animals with a shell.Lobster: Lobsters keep growing throughout life, shedding their shell many times, and can live decades.
Animals with a shell.Clam: A clam has two hinged shells, and the growth rings let scientists read its age, and ocean quahogs can live over 500 years.
Animals with a shell.Oyster: Oysters can change sex during their lives and filter many liters of water daily, and a pearl forms around an irritant.
Animals with a shell.Mussel: Mussels cling to rocks with strong silky threads called byssus, and they filter water.
Animals with a shell.Scallop: Scallops have dozens of tiny blue eyes along their shells, and they swim by clapping their shells.
Animals with a shell.Nautilus: Its spiral shell is divided into chambers that the animal uses to control buoyancy, and it has hardly changed in about 400 million years.
Animals with a shell.Hermit crab: It has no shell of its own, borrowing empty snail shells, and it swaps for a bigger one as it grows.
Animals with a shell.Barnacle: Barnacles are crustaceans, relatives of crabs, that glue themselves to rocks and boats, filtering food from water.
Animals with a shell.Slug: A slug is a snail with no shell, and it moves on a layer of slime.
Animals with a shell.Octopus: An octopus has no shell and a soft body, and can squeeze through any hole larger than its beak.
Animals with a shell.Jellyfish: A jellyfish has no shell, no bones, and no brain, and some species are over 95 percent water.
Animals with a shell.Starfish: Starfish have no shell, but a bumpy skeleton below the skin, and regrow lost arms.
Animals with a shell.Hedgehog: A hedgehog has spines, not a shell, and it has about 5,000 of them.
Animals with a shell.Porcupine: Porcupines have quills, not a shell, and they can't shoot them, contrary to myth.
Animals with a shell.Pangolin: A trap: it's armored with scales made of keratin, not a shell, and it rolls into a ball when threatened.
Animals with a shell.Earthworm: Earthworms have a soft, shell-free body and breathe through their skin.
Animals with a shell.Sea anemone: A sea anemone is soft-bodied, stinging, and shell-less, and it clings to rocks.
Animals with a shell.Frog: A frog has soft, thin skin, and no shell, and it can absorb water and breathe through its skin.
Animals with a shell.Lizard: Lizards have scales, not a shell, and many can drop their tails to escape predators.
Animals with a shell.Seal: A seal's insulating blubber, not a shell, keeps it warm in cold water.

Living things that glow in the dark.Firefly: Fireflies make light by a chemical reaction in their abdomen. Almost all the energy is released as light rather than heat, making it very efficient.
Living things that glow in the dark.Anglerfish: The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure, lit by symbiotic bacteria, in the dark deep sea. In some species, tiny males fuse permanently to the female.
Living things that glow in the dark.Glowworm: Glowworms are larvae of certain beetles or gnats. In New Zealand's caves, their glowing threads light up the ceilings like a starry sky.
Living things that glow in the dark.Lanternfish: Lanternfish are among the most abundant fish on Earth. They have light organs, and migrate to the surface at night.
Living things that glow in the dark.Firefly squid: The firefly squid of Japan lights up the sea off Toyama Bay in spring. Its body is dotted with light organs, called photophores.
Living things that glow in the dark.Dinoflagellate: Dinoflagellates are single-celled algae that flash blue when disturbed. They cause glowing waves, known as bioluminescent tides.
Living things that glow in the dark.Ghost mushroom: Ghost mushrooms, or Omphalotus nidiformis, glow a faint green on rotting wood in Australia. They are poisonous, so no one should eat them.
Living things that glow in the dark.Hatchetfish: Hatchetfish carry light organs on their underside, which match the dim light from above. This hides their silhouette from predators below.
Living things that glow in the dark.Lantern shark: The lantern shark is small, and has light organs along its belly. The velvet belly lanternshark is a well-known glowing shark.
Living things that glow in the dark.Cookiecutter shark: The cookiecutter shark glows green except on a dark collar, which may mimic a small fish. It takes round plugs of flesh from larger animals.
Living things that glow in the dark.Vampire squid: The vampire squid isn't a squid or vampire, and it glows to confuse. It can eject a cloud of glowing mucus instead of ink.
Living things that glow in the dark.House cat: A house cat's eyes shine at night from a reflective layer, the tapetum lucidum. That's reflection, not glowing: no light is produced.
Living things that glow in the dark.Electric eel: The electric eel produces electricity, up to about 600 volts, but it isn't luminous. And it's actually a knifefish, not a true eel.
Living things that glow in the dark.Ladybug: Ladybugs don't glow, though they do have bright warning colours. Some release smelly yellow fluid from their knees when threatened.
Living things that glow in the dark.Owl: Owls don't glow. Their feathers are specially fringed to dampen sound, and their eyes are fixed in place, so they swivel their necks about 270 degrees.
Living things that glow in the dark.Butterfly: Butterflies reflect light, but don't produce it. Their wings' colours often come from structure, not pigment.
Living things that glow in the dark.Bee: Bees don't glow, but they see ultraviolet light. Many flowers have UV patterns invisible to us that guide them to nectar.
Living things that glow in the dark.Goldfish: Goldfish don't glow. Their memory is far better than the three-second myth, and they can be trained to do tricks.
Living things that glow in the dark.Clownfish: Clownfish aren't luminous, but some fluoresce under blue light. They live safely among the stinging tentacles of anemones.
Living things that glow in the dark.Dragonfly: Dragonflies don't glow, but some have iridescent bodies. Their nymphs live underwater for years before they emerge.
Living things that glow in the dark.Seahorse: Seahorses don't make light, but some species do fluoresce when lit with blue light. This is reflection, not bioluminescence.
Living things that glow in the dark.Mosquito: Mosquitoes don't glow. They find hosts by sensing carbon dioxide and body heat.
Living things that glow in the dark.Starfish: Starfish are not known to be bioluminescent in general, though some brittle stars, their relatives, do produce light. True starfish lack it.
Living things that glow in the dark.Moth: Moths don't produce light, though they're drawn to it. Some can even jam bat sonar with ultrasonic clicks.

Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Sriracha: Sriracha is named after Si Racha, Thailand, and the American bottle with the rooster is made in California by Huy Fong Foods.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Tabasco: Tabasco comes from McIlhenny Company on Avery Island, Louisiana, and its peppers age in oak barrels for up to three years.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Harissa: Harissa is a Tunisian chili paste, flavored with garlic, caraway and coriander, and it's a staple across North Africa.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Sambal: Sambal is a chili paste from Indonesia and Malaysia, with several hundred varieties, and sambal oelek is the simplest, made of just chilies.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Gochujang: Gochujang is a fermented Korean red chili paste with a sweet, savory depth, made with glutinous rice and soybeans.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Piri piri: Piri piri is a hot sauce of African bird's eye chilies, brought into Portuguese cooking, and its name means 'pepper pepper' in Swahili.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Cholula: Cholula is a Mexican hot sauce, named for the ancient city of Cholula, and made with arbol and piquin peppers.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Frank's RedHot: Frank's RedHot is a Louisiana-style sauce, and was used in the original Buffalo wings recipe, according to the Anchor Bar story.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Chili crisp: Chili crisp is a crunchy Chinese chili oil with fried garlic and shallots, made famous worldwide by the Lao Gan Ma brand.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Zhoug: Zhoug is a fiery green herb and chili paste from Yemen, loved in Israel, with cilantro, cardamom and garlic.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Valentina: Valentina is a Mexican hot sauce in a bottle with a ribbon-like label, and it's a cheap, favorite topping on street food.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Ketchup: Ketchup is a sweet-and-sour tomato sauce, and it's not spicy; the early English version was made of mushrooms or fish.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Mayonnaise: Mayonnaise is a creamy emulsion of oil and egg yolk, so it isn't a hot sauce.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Hoisin: Hoisin is a sweet, thick Chinese bean sauce, so it's not a chili sauce.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Teriyaki: Teriyaki is sweet soy glaze, and it has no chili in it.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Ranch: Ranch dressing is a creamy buttermilk herb dressing, and the best-selling dressing in the US, but not spicy.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Tahini: Tahini is a sesame seed paste, so it has no chili heat.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Pesto: Pesto is a basil, pine nut and cheese sauce, so it has no heat to speak of.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Mint sauce: Mint sauce is a British sauce for lamb, made of mint, vinegar and sugar, and it's not a chili sauce.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Applesauce: Applesauce is just cooked apples, so it's gentle rather than spicy.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Tartar sauce: Tartar sauce is a mayonnaise with pickles and capers, and it's meant for fish, not for heat.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Béchamel: Béchamel is a creamy white sauce, so it isn't spicy at all.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Hollandaise: Hollandaise is a buttery egg sauce, mild and rich, so it is not a chili sauce.
Spicy chili sauces and pastes.Ponzu: Ponzu is a tangy citrus soy sauce from Japan, mild rather than fiery.

Things made from cocoa beans.Cocoa butter: The pale fat pressed from cocoa beans. It melts just below body temperature, which is why chocolate melts in your mouth.
Things made from cocoa beans.Hot chocolate: The Aztecs drank it cold, bitter and spiced. Europeans added sugar and heated it after the Spanish brought cocoa home.
Things made from cocoa beans.Cocoa nibs: Crushed, roasted cocoa bean pieces with no sugar added. They are crunchy and bitter, a bit like coffee beans.
Things made from cocoa beans.Nutella: Hazelnut spread whose cocoa content is small, and sugar is its top ingredient. Italian pastry maker Ferrero stretched scarce chocolate with hazelnuts after WWII.
Things made from cocoa beans.Ganache: Chocolate melted into warm cream. The French word can mean fool, and it is said to come from an apprentice's mistake.
Things made from cocoa beans.White chocolate: It has cocoa butter but no cocoa solids, which means it lacks the dark color and bitterness of other chocolates.
Things made from cocoa beans.Dark chocolate: Contains cocoa solids and cocoa butter, with little or no milk. Higher percentages mean more cocoa and less sugar.
Things made from cocoa beans.Milk chocolate: Invented in Switzerland in 1875 by Daniel Peter, who added powdered milk made by his neighbor Henri Nestle.
Things made from cocoa beans.Cocoa powder: What remains after most cocoa butter is pressed out. Dutch-process cocoa is treated with alkali to make it darker and milder.
Things made from cocoa beans.Chocolate milk: Sir Hans Sloane reportedly discovered cocoa mixed with milk in Jamaica in the 1600s and brought the recipe to England.
Things made from cocoa beans.Brigadeiro: Brazilian truffle of condensed milk, cocoa and butter rolled in sprinkles. Named after Brigadier Eduardo Gomes, a 1940s politician.
Things made from cocoa beans.Carob: Made from the pod of a Mediterranean tree. It looks like chocolate, but it is caffeine-free and naturally sweeter.
Things made from cocoa beans.Coffee: Roasted seeds of the coffee plant, not cocoa. Each is a different species from a different continent.
Things made from cocoa beans.Caramel: Sugar heated until it browns. No cocoa is involved, just sugar and heat.
Things made from cocoa beans.Toffee: Made from boiled sugar and butter. It is cooked until it reaches the hard crack stage.
Things made from cocoa beans.Butterscotch: Brown sugar and butter, with no scotch whisky involved. Its name likely comes from scotching, meaning scoring the candy.
Things made from cocoa beans.Vanilla: Seed pods of an orchid. It is the second most expensive spice after saffron, because every flower is hand pollinated.
Things made from cocoa beans.Licorice: From the root of a plant related to peas. Its compound glycyrrhizin tastes much sweeter than sugar.
Things made from cocoa beans.Maple syrup: Boiled sap from sugar maple trees. It takes roughly 40 liters of sap to make one liter of syrup.
Things made from cocoa beans.Dulce de leche: Milk slowly simmered with sugar until golden and thick. Argentines and Uruguayans claim it.
Things made from cocoa beans.Marzipan: Ground almonds and sugar. A chocolate coating does not make it chocolate.
Things made from cocoa beans.Halva: A sweet from sesame paste and sugar. Chocolate swirls are sometimes added but are not essential.
Things made from cocoa beans.Cola: Flavored originally with kola nuts, not cocoa, though both contain caffeine-like stimulants. Early Coca-Cola also contained coca leaf extract.
Things made from cocoa beans.Shea butter: A fat from the nuts of an African tree. It is sometimes used in chocolate but is not made from cocoa.

Rivers of Europe.Danube: Europe's second-longest river, flowing through or past ten countries, more than any other river in the world, and four of its capitals sit on its banks.
Rivers of Europe.Rhine: Flows from the Alps through Germany to the Netherlands, and carries more cargo than any other European river. Its Loreley rock is a folklore landmark.
Rivers of Europe.Seine: Runs through Paris, with its banks on UNESCO's World Heritage list. Its islands, including the Île de la Cité, are where Paris began.
Rivers of Europe.Thames: London's river, only about 346 km long. Despite being short, the Romans founded Londinium on its banks.
Rivers of Europe.Loire: France's longest river, flanked by hundreds of Renaissance châteaux. It's known as the Garden of France.
Rivers of Europe.Elbe: Flows through Dresden and Hamburg into the North Sea. Its name is of Germanic origin, and it is the site of a war-era meeting between American and Soviet troops in 1945.
Rivers of Europe.Po: Italy's longest river, running across the north from the Alps to the Adriatic. Its plain is Italy's farming heartland.
Rivers of Europe.Tiber: The river of Rome, in legend where the infant Romulus and Remus were found. Rome's early power was built around its crossing.
Rivers of Europe.Volga: Europe's longest river, over 3,500 km, flowing through Russia to the Caspian Sea. It's called Mother Volga.
Rivers of Europe.Vistula: Poland's longest river, flowing through Kraków and Warsaw to the Baltic. It's one of the few big European rivers still largely unregulated.
Rivers of Europe.Oder: A river forming part of the Polish-German border since 1945, flowing north to the Baltic. It shares its flood-prone course with Poland.
Rivers of Europe.Tagus: The Iberian Peninsula's longest river, flowing from Spain to Lisbon, where it widens before reaching the Atlantic.
Rivers of Europe.Dnieper: A river flowing through Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, to the Black Sea. Its Chernobyl-area tributaries were hit by the 1986 nuclear accident.
Rivers of Europe.Nile: A trap: it is the world's longest river, at about 6,650 km, but it runs through Africa, not Europe.
Rivers of Europe.Amazon: A trap: the world's largest river by volume, carrying more water than the next seven combined. It is South American.
Rivers of Europe.Ganges: A trap: India's sacred river, where millions bathe at festivals. It flows through Asia, not Europe.
Rivers of Europe.Mekong: A trap: a Southeast Asian river that passes through six countries. It is not European.
Rivers of Europe.Yukon: A trap: a river of Alaska and Canada's Yukon, famous from the Klondike Gold Rush. It is not European.
Rivers of Europe.Zambezi: A trap: a southern African river, home of Victoria Falls. It is not a European river.
Rivers of Europe.Euphrates: A trap: with the Tigris, it watered ancient Mesopotamia, so it is Asian, not European.
Rivers of Europe.Orinoco: A trap: a South American river crossing Venezuela and Colombia. It is not European.
Rivers of Europe.Hudson: A trap: a New York river named for explorer Henry Hudson, who sailed it in 1609. It is not European.
Rivers of Europe.Colorado: A trap: the river that carved the Grand Canyon in the American Southwest. It is not European.
Rivers of Europe.Indus: A trap: Asian river from Tibet through Pakistan, which gave India its name. It is not European.

Bones in the human body.Femur: The thigh bone is the longest and strongest bone in the body, and makes up roughly a quarter of your height.
Bones in the human body.Tibia: The shinbone carries most of your weight below the knee. Its name is Latin for flute, since early flutes were carved from such bones.
Bones in the human body.Fibula: The slender bone beside the shin carries little weight. Its name is Latin for brooch, since it resembles a clasp pin.
Bones in the human body.Humerus: The upper arm bone. Its funny bone nerve, the ulnar nerve, passes behind its elbow, a pun on the word humorous.
Bones in the human body.Radius: One of the two forearm bones, on the thumb side. It rotates around the ulna, which lets you turn your palm up and down.
Bones in the human body.Ulna: The forearm bone on the pinky side. Its top end forms the pointed bony tip of your elbow.
Bones in the human body.Patella: The kneecap is Latin for small plate. A baby is born with soft cartilage there, and it hardens into bone over several years.
Bones in the human body.Clavicle: The collarbone is the most commonly broken bone, and is the only long bone that lies horizontally. Its name means little key.
Bones in the human body.Scapula: The shoulder blade is a flat triangular bone that floats on the back, held only by muscles. It is not attached by a joint to the ribs.
Bones in the human body.Sternum: The breastbone is a flat bone at the center of the chest. CPR compresses it to squeeze the heart.
Bones in the human body.Mandible: The jawbone is the only movable bone in the skull, apart from tiny ear bones, and the strongest bone of the face.
Bones in the human body.Coccyx: The tailbone is a leftover of our ancestors' tails. It's made of several tiny fused vertebrae.
Bones in the human body.Stapes: The stirrup bone in your middle ear is the smallest in the body, about 3 millimeters long, and passes sound to the inner ear.
Bones in the human body.Hyoid: A small U-shaped bone in the neck, unique because it isn't joined to any other bone. It anchors the tongue and helps in speech.
Bones in the human body.Biceps: A trap: it's a muscle, not a bone. The name means two heads, since it attaches at two points on the shoulder.
Bones in the human body.Triceps: A trap: a muscle, not a bone. It has three heads and makes up about two thirds of your upper arm's bulk.
Bones in the human body.Tendon: A trap: a tendon links muscle to bone, but isn't a bone. The Achilles tendon is the thickest in the body.
Bones in the human body.Cartilage: A trap: it's softer and more flexible than bone. Your ears and nose tip are made of it, and a baby's skeleton starts mostly as cartilage.
Bones in the human body.Aorta: A trap: it's the body's largest artery, not a bone. It's about as wide as a garden hose.
Bones in the human body.Ligament: A trap: ligaments join bone to bone but are not bone themselves. The ACL in the knee is a famous one.
Bones in the human body.Spleen: A trap: it's an organ, not a bone. It filters old red blood cells and stores immune cells.
Bones in the human body.Deltoid: A trap: the rounded shoulder muscle, not a bone. It's named for the Greek letter delta, which it resembles in shape.
Bones in the human body.Pancreas: A trap: it's a gland, not a bone. It makes insulin, which regulates blood sugar.
Bones in the human body.Cornea: A trap: the clear front surface of the eye, not a bone. It has no blood vessels, getting oxygen directly from the air.

Electromagnetic waves.Radio waves: The longest waves in the electromagnetic spectrum, from centimeters to kilometers; they carry radio, TV and mobile signals.
Electromagnetic waves.Microwaves: Waves a few centimeters long; ovens use them to shake water molecules, and the leftover glow of the Big Bang is microwave too.
Electromagnetic waves.Infrared: Heat that you feel as warmth but cannot see; TV remotes use it, and snakes such as pit vipers can sense it.
Electromagnetic waves.Visible light: A tiny sliver of the spectrum, wavelengths of about 400 to 700 nanometers, and it's the only part human eyes can see.
Electromagnetic waves.Ultraviolet: Shorter than violet light, and it causes sunburn; bees can see it, and flowers have patterns invisible to us.
Electromagnetic waves.X-rays: Discovered by Wilhelm Roentgen in 1895; his first image was of his wife's hand with her ring.
Electromagnetic waves.Gamma rays: The most energetic electromagnetic waves, from nuclear decay and exploding stars, and they can pass through thick lead.
Electromagnetic waves.Wi-Fi signals: Home Wi-Fi is just microwaves at about 2.4 or 5 GHz, so your router is a low-power radio.
Electromagnetic waves.Radar: Radio waves bounced off objects to find them; it was key in Britain's defense during World War II.
Electromagnetic waves.Sunlight: A mix of infrared, visible and ultraviolet light, which takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.
Electromagnetic waves.Laser light: Light where all waves are in step and the same color, which lets it travel in a narrow beam to the Moon and back.
Electromagnetic waves.Sound waves: A trap: sound is vibrating matter, not electromagnetic, so it needs air or water and can't cross a vacuum.
Electromagnetic waves.Ultrasound: A trap: sound too high for human ears, so it's mechanical vibration, as used by bats and in pregnancy scans.
Electromagnetic waves.Seismic waves: A trap: vibrations through the Earth after quakes, so they're mechanical waves, not electromagnetic.
Electromagnetic waves.Ocean waves: A trap: energy moving through water, mostly driven by wind, so they need a medium, unlike light.
Electromagnetic waves.Shock waves: A trap: a sudden pressure front in a material, as in a sonic boom, and not an electromagnetic wave.
Electromagnetic waves.Alpha particles: A trap: two protons and two neutrons ejected from atoms, so they're matter, which a sheet of paper can stop.
Electromagnetic waves.Beta particles: A trap: fast electrons from radioactive decay, so they're particles, not waves of light.
Electromagnetic waves.Sonar: A trap: it uses sound pulses underwater, not radio, and that's why ships use sonar in the sea, where radar fails.
Electromagnetic waves.Echoes: A trap: reflected sound, so it's mechanical, and doesn't exist in space where there is no air.
Electromagnetic waves.Ripples: A trap: ripples on water are mechanical waves in a liquid, not electromagnetic.
Electromagnetic waves.Gravitational waves: A trap: ripples in spacetime itself, first detected in 2015, and they aren't electromagnetic, though they travel at light speed.
Electromagnetic waves.Tsunami: A trap: a wave of water, so mechanical, not electromagnetic, however far it travels.
Electromagnetic waves.Cosmic rays: A trap: despite the name they are mostly fast protons and atomic nuclei, so particles instead of electromagnetic waves.

Branches of physics.Mechanics: The study of motion and forces, the field Newton founded, and it still guides everything from bridges to space probes.
Branches of physics.Thermodynamics: It deals with heat, energy and entropy, and its second law says disorder in the universe always tends to increase.
Branches of physics.Optics: The study of light, lenses and vision, which led to the telescope and microscope, and it helped reveal that light is a wave.
Branches of physics.Acoustics: The physics of sound, including the way concert halls are designed, and why a sonic boom happens when something outruns its own sound.
Branches of physics.Electromagnetism: The union of electricity and magnetism, joined in the 1860s by Maxwell, explains light itself as an electromagnetic wave.
Branches of physics.Quantum mechanics: The physics of the very small, where particles can act like waves, and Einstein himself disliked its randomness, saying God does not play dice.
Branches of physics.Relativity: Einstein's theories reshaped time and space: moving clocks tick slower, and your phone's GPS must correct for it.
Branches of physics.Nuclear physics: It studies the atom's core, from fission in power plants to fusion in stars, and it began with Becquerel's accidental discovery of radioactivity.
Branches of physics.Astrophysics: The physics of stars, galaxies and the universe, which uses the laws from labs to explain why the Sun shines.
Branches of physics.Fluid dynamics: The science of how liquids and gases flow covers weather, blood flow and why a spinning ball curves through the air.
Branches of physics.Particle physics: It hunts for the smallest building blocks, such as quarks, and the Large Hadron Collider found the Higgs boson in 2012.
Branches of physics.Botany: The study of plants, from mosses to oaks, and it's a branch of biology, not physics.
Branches of physics.Zoology: The study of animals, which is part of biology, not physics, and its name comes from Greek for living being.
Branches of physics.Ecology: The science of how living things interact with their environment, which belongs to biology, not physics.
Branches of physics.Genetics: The study of heredity and DNA, which is biology, and it began with Mendel's peas.
Branches of physics.Geology: The study of Earth's rocks and structure, an Earth science that borrows physics but is its own field.
Branches of physics.Anatomy: The study of the body's structure, which is part of biology and medicine, not physics.
Branches of physics.Organic chemistry: The study of carbon-based compounds is chemistry, the base of fuels and plastics, not physics.
Branches of physics.Biochemistry: The chemistry of living things, a mix of biology and chemistry, not a physics branch.
Branches of physics.Taxonomy: The science of classifying living things, founded by Linnaeus, which is biology, not physics.
Branches of physics.Microbiology: The study of microscopic life such as bacteria, which belongs to biology, not physics.
Branches of physics.Paleontology: The study of fossils and ancient life, a field mixing geology and biology, not physics.
Branches of physics.Entomology: The study of insects, the most diverse animal group, which is biology, not physics.
Branches of physics.Mycology: The study of fungi, including mushrooms and molds, a part of biology, not physics.

Optical devices you look through.Telescope: Galileo's 1609 version was cobbled together from lenses, and he used it to spot Jupiter's four big moons. It was invented by Dutch spectacle makers.
Optical devices you look through.Microscope: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek used handmade single-lens microscopes in the 1670s to become the first to see bacteria, which he called 'animalcules'.
Optical devices you look through.Binoculars: Two small telescopes joined side by side. Prisms inside flip the image upright and let the tubes be shorter.
Optical devices you look through.Periscope: Mirrors or prisms let you see over or around obstacles. Submarines have used them since before World War I.
Optical devices you look through.Kaleidoscope: Invented by David Brewster in 1816. Just a few mirrors and bits of colored glass produce endless symmetric patterns.
Optical devices you look through.Magnifying glass: A single convex lens that makes things look larger. Focused sunlight through one can start a fire, so don't leave it on a sunny windowsill.
Optical devices you look through.Spyglass: A small handheld telescope that slides shut. Captain Cook and other explorers used them to scout coasts from the deck of their ships.
Optical devices you look through.Monocle: A single eyeglass lens worn in one eye. It was fashionable among 19th-century gentlemen, and held in place by the eye socket muscles.
Optical devices you look through.Viewfinder: The part of a camera you look through to frame a shot. Reflex cameras use a mirror so you see the exact image the lens sees.
Optical devices you look through.Peephole: A tiny wide-angle lens in a door that lets you see out while others can't see in. It shows a distorted fisheye view.
Optical devices you look through.Loupe: A small magnifier jewelers hold to the eye to inspect gems. A typical one magnifies ten times, the standard for grading diamonds.
Optical devices you look through.Stethoscope: A trap: you listen with it rather than look through it. René Laennec invented it in 1816 to avoid pressing his ear to a woman's chest.
Optical devices you look through.Oscilloscope: It displays electrical signals as waves on a screen. You look at it rather than through it, with no lens involved.
Optical devices you look through.Horoscope: A trap: it looks like a '-scope', but it's astrology. The name comes from Greek for 'observer of the hour'.
Optical devices you look through.Seismograph: Records ground shaking as a wiggly line. Rather than seeing anything, it measures earthquakes.
Optical devices you look through.Barometer: Measures air pressure, which falls before storms. Evangelista Torricelli invented it in 1643 using a tube of mercury.
Optical devices you look through.Thermometer: Gives the temperature, not an image. The Fahrenheit scale was set by Daniel Fahrenheit using a mercury version in the 1710s.
Optical devices you look through.Gyroscope: A spinning wheel that holds its orientation. It keeps airplanes and spacecraft steady, and is not an optical device.
Optical devices you look through.Metronome: A ticking device for musicians that keeps steady time. It does not involve lenses in any way.
Optical devices you look through.Compass: Points to magnetic north using a magnetized needle. It was invented in China, and you read it, not look through it.
Optical devices you look through.Hourglass: Marks time with falling sand. It was a common timer at sea, since waves don't disturb it as they do pendulum clocks.
Optical devices you look through.Speedometer: Shows how fast a vehicle moves with a dial. It is a gauge you read, not a lens you look through.
Optical devices you look through.Pendulum: A weight swinging from a fixed point, whose swing time depends on its length. Galileo noticed it in a swinging church lamp.
Optical devices you look through.Protractor: A semicircle used to measure angles. It's a measuring tool, not a viewing device.

Legumes (members of the pea family).Peanut: A legume, not a nut. The flower stalk bends down after pollination and pushes the pod underground, where the peanut ripens.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Chickpea: One of the world's oldest cultivated crops. Cooking its water makes aquafaba, which whips like egg whites and is used in vegan meringues.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Lentil: Among the earliest domesticated crops, grown in the Near East for around 9,000 years. The lens takes its name from the lentil's shape.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Soybean: A legume, and the source of tofu, soy milk and soy sauce. It's one of the few plant foods that provides all the essential amino acids.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Kidney bean: Raw or undercooked kidney beans contain a toxin, phytohaemagglutinin, that can make you very ill. Boiling them thoroughly destroys it.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Pea: Gregor Mendel's pea plants helped him uncover the basic laws of heredity. The pea is a legume, and that's why this family is named after it.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Green bean: Eaten pod and all, it's a legume picked young. Green beans are the same species as kidney beans, just harvested before the seeds mature.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Alfalfa: A legume grown mainly as livestock feed. Its name comes from Arabic and means roughly 'father of all foods', and its roots reach deep for water.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Clover: Clover is a legume whose roots host bacteria that turn air nitrogen into fertilizer. Farmers have used it to renew soil for centuries.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Black bean: A legume widely used across Latin America. Its dark skin has anthocyanin pigments, the same family as in blueberries.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Licorice: Real licorice comes from the root of a pea-family plant. Its sweet compound, glycyrrhizin, is far sweeter than sugar and can raise blood pressure if overeaten.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Tamarind: A tropical tree in the pea family, with sticky, tangy pulp in a brown pod. It's a key ingredient in Worcestershire sauce.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Carob: A pea-family tree whose pods are ground into a cocoa substitute. Its seeds were once used as a unit of weight, giving us the word carat.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Almond: A drupe seed and a close relative of the peach, not a legume. The 'nut' is the kernel inside a hard pit.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Walnut: A true nut-like seed from a tree in the walnut family, no relation to legumes. The wrinkled kernel's shape is a famous brain lookalike.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Cashew: Related to mangoes and poison ivy, not to peas. The nut hangs outside the cashew apple, and its shell contains an irritating oil.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Corn: A grass, not a legume. Native Americans often grew it with beans and squash, where the beans fix nitrogen the corn needs.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Rice: A grass, so it belongs with wheat and corn rather than peas. It feeds more than half the world's population.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Quinoa: A seed from a plant related to spinach and beets, not to peas. It's sometimes called a pseudocereal because it's used like grain.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Coffee bean: Despite the name, it's a seed from the coffee cherry, from a plant in the madder family. It isn't a legume at all.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Cocoa bean: The seed of the cacao tree, which belongs to the mallow family. It isn't a true bean, though it's called one.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Vanilla bean: The cured pod of an orchid, not a legume. Vanilla is the world's second most expensive spice after saffron.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Jelly bean: A candy, with no plant roots at all. Its name comes from its bean shape and its soft sugar-gel center.
Legumes (members of the pea family).Castor bean: The seed of a spurge-family plant, and extremely toxic, as it contains ricin. It's no legume, despite the name, though castor oil comes from it.

Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Blue whale: The largest animal ever known, reaching about 30 meters. Its heart is the size of a small car, and its call can be heard from miles away.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Humpback whale: Males sing complex songs that change from year to year and spread across populations. They also blow nets of bubbles to corral fish.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Orca: The killer whale is actually the largest dolphin. Different pods have different diets and dialects, passed down like cultural traditions.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Sperm whale: The biggest toothed predator, diving over a kilometer deep for squid. Its head holds spermaceti, a waxy fluid that's linked to buoyancy and sound.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Beluga: A white Arctic whale nicknamed the canary of the sea for its chirps and whistles. Its flexible neck lets it turn its head, which most whales can't do.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Narwhal: The male's 'horn' is actually a spiralled tooth that can grow over 2 meters. It's packed with nerve endings that sense the water.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Bottlenose dolphin: Bottlenose dolphins call each other by individual signature whistles, much like names. They're also famous for riding the bow waves of boats.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Porpoise: Smaller and shyer than dolphins, with spade-shaped teeth rather than cone-shaped ones. The harbor porpoise is among the smallest cetaceans.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Minke whale: One of the smallest baleen whales, and the most numerous. Some Antarctic minkes have been seen to flip over to feed while swimming.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Gray whale: It migrates up to about 20,000 kilometers each year, one of the longest of any mammal. It feeds by scooping up sediment off the seabed.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Pilot whale: A large dolphin with a rounded head, living in tight family pods. Females keep helping raise young long after they can no longer breed.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Whale shark: Although it's called a whale, it's the biggest fish in the sea. It breathes through gills and filters plankton, so it's no cetacean.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Manatee: A gentle plant-eater that's a sea cow, not a cetacean. Its closest living relatives are elephants.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Dugong: A grazing marine mammal related to manatees, and thought to be the origin of mermaid legends. It's a sirenian, not a cetacean.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Walrus: A tusked marine mammal that can weigh over a tonne. It belongs with seals and sea lions, not whales.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Seal: A seal is a pinniped with flippers and whiskers, while whales are cetaceans. Seals still come ashore to give birth.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Sea lion: Sea lions have visible ear flaps and can walk on their flippers on land. That sets them apart from true seals, and both are pinnipeds.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Sea otter: The smallest marine mammal, with the densest fur of any animal. It sometimes holds hands with others while it sleeps, so as not to drift.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Basking shark: A giant filter-feeder that can reach about 10 meters. It's a fish with gills, so not related to whales.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Manta ray: A huge, graceful ray with wings that span several meters. It's a cartilaginous fish, not a mammal.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Elephant seal: Males have trunk-like noses and can weigh over 3 tonnes. They're pinnipeds, so the nearest relatives are other seals.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Leopard seal: A spotted Antarctic predator that hunts penguins. It's a seal, not a whale.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Penguin: A flightless seabird that swims with its wings. It's a bird, which lays eggs, unlike any cetacean.
Cetaceans (whales, dolphins and porpoise.Hippo: Its closest living relatives are actually whales. Even so, a hippo is a land and river dweller, not a cetacean itself.

Real chemical elements (not fictional).Rubidium: Rubidium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water, and its name comes from the Latin for deep red, after the color of its spectral lines.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Ytterbium: Ytterbium is named after Ytterby, a Swedish village that gave names to four elements, which is the record for a single place.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Dysprosium: Dysprosium's name comes from the Greek for 'hard to get', and it is vital in the magnets of electric motors and wind turbines.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Praseodymium: Praseodymium is named from Greek for 'green twin', and gives a green tint to glass and welding goggles.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Molybdenum: Molybdenum is used to strengthen steel, and its name comes from the Greek for lead, since it was mistaken for it.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Rhodium: Rhodium is one of the most valuable metals per ounce, and it is used in car catalytic converters.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Hafnium: Hafnium was named after Copenhagen, using the Latin name Hafnia, and is used in control rods in nuclear reactors.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Thulium: Thulium is among the rarest of the rare earths, and is named after Thule, an ancient name for Scandinavia.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Lutetium: Lutetium is named for Lutetia, the Roman name for Paris, and is used in PET scanners.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Gadolinium: Gadolinium is used as a contrast agent in MRI scans, and is named in honor of the chemist Johan Gadolin.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Promethium: Promethium is radioactive, with no stable isotopes, and it is named after the Titan Prometheus, who stole fire.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Unobtainium: Unobtainium is a joke term for any impossibly rare engineering material, and Avatar made it a movie mineral.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Adamantium: Adamantium is Marvel's unbreakable metal, famously bonded to Wolverine's skeleton, and it is not a real element.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Vibranium: Vibranium is Marvel's metal in Black Panther's suit, which absorbs vibrations and is mined in Wakanda.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Kryptonite: Kryptonite is the green mineral from Superman's home planet which weakens him, and was first created for a radio show in the 1940s.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Mithril: Mithril is a light and strong silvery metal in Tolkien's Middle-earth, and Frodo wore a shirt made of it.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Trilithium: Trilithium is a Star Trek compound, used in a weapon that could destroy a star, and not a real element.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Byzanium: Byzanium is a made-up metal from science fiction, and it is not on the periodic table.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Carbonite: Carbonite is the Star Wars substance used to freeze Han Solo, though the name sounds like a real mineral.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Naquadah: Naquadah is a fictional element in Stargate, a rare mineral that powers the gates, and it is not real.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Tiberium: Tiberium is the alien crystal in the Command and Conquer games, which spreads across the planet.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Element Zero: Element Zero is a fictional substance in Mass Effect, which makes faster-than-light travel possible.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Octiron: Octiron is Discworld's eighth magical element, which is the color octarine, and not on any real periodic table.
Real chemical elements (not fictional).Administratium: Administratium is a satirical element, and the joke says it makes a reaction take place without being involved in it.

Harry Potter characters.Hermione: Her name comes from Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale, and Rowling chose it as an uncommon name so girls like her wouldn't be teased. She's the trio's brains.
Harry Potter characters.Dumbledore: His first name Albus means white, and 'dumbledore' is an old English word for bumblebee. Rowling said she imagined him humming.
Harry Potter characters.Snape: Severus Snape's loyalty is the series' biggest twist, revealed through his memories. The name Snape is a real English surname and place name.
Harry Potter characters.Hagrid: Rubeus Hagrid is half-giant, gamekeeper of Hogwarts, and delivers Harry's letter. His love of dangerous creatures gets him in trouble.
Harry Potter characters.Voldemort: His name is French for 'flight of death', and 'Tom Marvolo Riddle' is an anagram of 'I am Lord Voldemort'.
Harry Potter characters.Dobby: This house-elf is freed from the Malfoys when Harry tricks Lucius into handing him a sock. He's a free elf who loves socks.
Harry Potter characters.Neville: Neville Longbottom starts as the clumsy boy and becomes a hero who destroys Nagini, Voldemort's snake, with Gryffindor's sword.
Harry Potter characters.Sirius Black: Sirius is also the name of the brightest star in the night sky, the Dog Star. He can turn into a big black dog.
Harry Potter characters.Luna Lovegood: Her name echoes the moon and is a clue to her dreamy personality. She's a Ravenclaw who believes in creatures others don't.
Harry Potter characters.Draco Malfoy: Draco is Latin for dragon and the name of a constellation. Malfoy hints at 'bad faith' in French.
Harry Potter characters.Gandalf: Gandalf is a wizard from Tolkien's Middle-earth, not Hogwarts. His name comes from a Norse dwarf-list in the Edda.
Harry Potter characters.Frodo: Frodo is a hobbit in The Lord of the Rings by Tolkien. He's from the Shire, not the wizarding world.
Harry Potter characters.Merlin: Merlin is the wizard of Arthurian legend, centuries older than Harry Potter, though Hogwarts students swear by his name.
Harry Potter characters.Aragorn: Aragorn is the heir of Gondor in Lord of the Rings. He's a Tolkien hero, and Harry Potter has no such king.
Harry Potter characters.Bilbo: Bilbo Baggins is the hero of The Hobbit, which Tolkien published in 1937. He is no Hogwarts student.
Harry Potter characters.Saruman: Saruman is the corrupted wizard in Tolkien's world. Not at Hogwarts, though both worlds have a wizard who goes bad.
Harry Potter characters.Legolas: Legolas is an elf archer in Lord of the Rings. Like Hogwarts, Middle-earth has elves, but of a very different kind.
Harry Potter characters.Elrond: Elrond is the elf lord of Rivendell in Tolkien's tales. He isn't part of Rowling's world.
Harry Potter characters.Gollum: Gollum is the creature obsessed with the Ring in Tolkien's world. He's no Harry Potter character.
Harry Potter characters.Percy Jackson: Percy Jackson is Rick Riordan's demigod hero, son of Poseidon. Not Hogwarts, though a Weasley is called Percy too.
Harry Potter characters.Eragon: Eragon is a young dragon rider in Christopher Paolini's series, written when the author was a teenager.
Harry Potter characters.Aslan: Aslan is the lion king of Narnia in C.S. Lewis's books. He's not from the Hogwarts story.
Harry Potter characters.Glinda: Glinda is the Good Witch in L. Frank Baum's Oz books. She's not in Harry Potter, though both worlds have witches.
Harry Potter characters.Mr. Tumnus: Mr. Tumnus is a faun in Narnia who meets Lucy beside a lamppost. He's no Hogwarts figure.

Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).How you doin'?: Joey Tribbiani's pickup line on Friends. Matt LeBlanc played him so well that the character got his own, shorter-lived spin-off, Joey.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).Bazinga: Sheldon Cooper's way of announcing a prank on The Big Bang Theory. The show ran for twelve seasons.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).D'oh!: Homer Simpson's grunt of frustration was added to the Oxford English Dictionary in 2001. It is a cartoon sitcom's mark.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).Did I do that?: Steve Urkel's line on Family Matters after another accident. Urkel was meant as a one-off guest but became the show's star.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).Dy-no-mite!: Jimmie Walker's J.J. shouted it on Good Times, a 1970s sitcom about a Chicago family. It was the show's best-known line.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).Yada yada yada: Seinfeld used it for glossing over a story's details. The phrase grew so popular it entered everyday speech.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).No soup for you!: The Soup Nazi's ruling on Seinfeld was inspired by a real New York soup shop owner, Al Yeganeh.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).Nanu nanu: Robin Williams as an alien in Mork and Mindy greeted people this way, and it came with a split-finger salute.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).Cool cool cool: Jake Peralta's filler phrase on Brooklyn Nine-Nine. It is a way of saying everything is fine when it isn't.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).Eat my shorts: Bart Simpson's retort helped make The Simpsons a merchandise sensation in 1990; some schools banned T-shirts bearing it.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).We were on a break!: Ross Geller's favorite defense on Friends about his split with Rachel. The argument is never really settled.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).I'll be back: From The Terminator (1984), a film. Arnold Schwarzenegger reportedly wanted to say I will be back, as he found contractions hard for a machine.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).Hasta la vista baby: From Terminator 2, a film, where it is the Terminator's farewell. Arnold's line is a movie quote, not a sitcom catchphrase.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).You talkin' to me?: Robert De Niro reportedly improvised it in the Taxi Driver mirror scene. It belongs to a 1976 film, not a sitcom.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).Show me the money!: Cuba Gooding Jr. shouts it in Jerry Maguire, which won him an Oscar. It is a film line, never a sitcom's.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).E.T. phone home: The little alien's line in Spielberg's 1982 film. It topped the box office, but it is a film line, not a sitcom's.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).Just keep swimming: Dory's mantra in Finding Nemo, an animated film; it fits the kids' movie, not a sitcom.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).I see dead people: The boy's whispered line in The Sixth Sense, a 1999 film. Its twist ending made it a movie classic, not a sitcom quote.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).Hakuna Matata: From The Lion King, a film. It means no worries in Swahili, and the song is a film number rather than a sitcom's catchphrase.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).Yippee-ki-yay: John McClane's line in Die Hard, a film. Many consider it a Christmas movie, but it isn't a sitcom line.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).Why so serious?: The Joker's line in The Dark Knight, a film. Heath Ledger won a posthumous Oscar for the role, not for a sitcom.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).I am Groot: Groot's only line in Guardians of the Galaxy, a film. It sounds like a catchphrase, but it comes from a movie, not a sitcom.
Catchphrases from TV sitcoms (not films).Wax on wax off: Mr. Miyagi teaches this in The Karate Kid, a 1984 film. It's a movie line, not from a sitcom.
Sean Connery introduced it in the 1962 film Dr. No. It's a movie line, not a sitcom's.

Bears from film and TV.Paddington: Michael Bond's marmalade-loving bear came from darkest Peru. He keeps an emergency sandwich under his hat.
Bears from film and TV.Baloo: The sloth bear in Disney's The Jungle Book sings The Bare Necessities, and his movie voice was Phil Harris.
Bears from film and TV.Winnie the Pooh: Named after a real Canadian black bear, Winnipeg, who lived at London Zoo and belonged to a Canadian soldier.
Bears from film and TV.Lotso: The strawberry-scented villain of Toy Story 3 is a pink plush bear, voiced by Ned Beatty.
Bears from film and TV.Yogi Bear: Hanna-Barbera's Jellystone bear is 'smarter than the average bear' and loves stealing pic-a-nic baskets.
Bears from film and TV.Ted: The foul-mouthed teddy bear in Seth MacFarlane's film is voiced by MacFarlane himself, who also does Peter Griffin.
Bears from film and TV.Koda: The young bear in Disney's Brother Bear is an orphan, and the film features Phil Collins songs.
Bears from film and TV.Fozzie Bear: The Muppets' stand-up comic is famous for his 'wocka wocka' catchphrase, and his jokes get met with heckling by Statler and Waldorf.
Bears from film and TV.Little John: In Disney's 1973 Robin Hood, the bear is voiced by Phil Harris, who also voiced Baloo, and he's Robin's best pal.
Bears from film and TV.Po: Kung Fu Panda's hero is a giant panda, and pandas are in fact bears, despite the slightly different look.
Bears from film and TV.Mor'du: The cursed bear prince in Brave is a huge terrifying bear who bites off the Fergus's leg.
Bears from film and TV.Boo Boo: Yogi's pint-sized sidekick, who tries to keep him out of trouble with Ranger Smith, and who wears a bow tie.
Bears from film and TV.Buster Moon: A koala, not a bear: Sing's theater owner is a marsupial, and koalas are often miscalled 'koala bears' though they aren't related to bears.
Bears from film and TV.Rocket: A raccoon, not a bear. Raccoons are in the procyonid family, and are distant cousins at best of bears, despite the resemblance.
Bears from film and TV.Meeko: Pocahontas's mischievous sidekick is a raccoon. Like Rocket, he shares a similar bandit face with no bear lineage.
Bears from film and TV.Tigger: A tiger, not a bear: Pooh's bouncy pal in the Hundred Acre Wood declares that the most wonderful thing about Tiggers is that he's the only one.
Bears from film and TV.Eeyore: A gloomy donkey, not a bear, who famously loses his tail, which Pooh and friends nail back on in the books.
Bears from film and TV.Gloria: A hippo from Madagascar, voiced by Jada Pinkett Smith, so not a bear despite her friendly bulk.
Bears from film and TV.Sid: A sloth, not a bear: Ice Age's Sid is a giant ground sloth, a relative of today's tree sloths, and nothing like Baloo the sloth bear.
Bears from film and TV.Scrat: The acorn-chasing 'saber-toothed squirrel' of Ice Age is a rodent-like creature. Scrat started as a one-gag character, and became a star.
Bears from film and TV.Bagheera: A black panther, not a bear. In The Jungle Book he is Baloo's partner in guarding Mowgli.
Bears from film and TV.Master Shifu: A red panda, so not a bear. Red pandas belong to their own family, and are closer to raccoons and weasels than to giant pandas.
Bears from film and TV.Simba: A lion cub who becomes king, and so not a bear. His name is Swahili for 'lion'.
Bears from film and TV.Diego: A saber-toothed cat in Ice Age. Smilodon was not a true tiger, and the ones that lived there had no relation to bears.

Songs from The Sound of Music.Do-Re-Mi: Maria teaches the von Trapp children the musical scale, based on a medieval system that gave each note a syllable.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Edelweiss: Written for the show in 1959, it was among Oscar Hammerstein's last lyrics, and many believe it to be an Austrian folk song.
Songs from The Sound of Music.My Favorite Things: The song became a jazz standard after John Coltrane recorded it in 1960, and a Christmas favorite as well.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Climb Ev'ry Mountain: The Mother Abbess sings this stirring anthem urging Maria to follow her dreams, and it closes the film.
Songs from The Sound of Music.The Lonely Goatherd: The yodeling puppet number was originally sung by the Baroness in the stage version, and the film gave it to the children.
Songs from The Sound of Music.So Long Farewell: The children sing it at the von Trapp party, leaving the room one at a time in a clever staged goodnight.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Maria: The nuns ask 'How do you solve a problem like Maria?' in this comic number about the troublesome young novice.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Something Good: Written specially for the 1965 film, it is sung by Maria and the Captain, and Richard Rodgers wrote its words and music.
Songs from The Sound of Music.I Have Confidence: Another song added only for the film, Rodgers wrote both words and music after Hammerstein's death.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Tonight: Trap: this is a love ballad from West Side Story, not The Sound of Music.
Songs from The Sound of Music.America: Trap: it is a lively number from West Side Story, with a Latin beat.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Memory: Trap: it is from Cats and sung by Grizabella, nothing to do with the Alps.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Tomorrow: Trap: Annie sings it, and it has no link to the von Trapps.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Summer Nights: Trap: it is from Grease, not The Sound of Music.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Over the Rainbow: Trap: from The Wizard of Oz, and has no ties to the Austrian Alps.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Defying Gravity: Trap: it is the iconic finale of Act One in Wicked.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Cabaret: Trap: it is the title song of Cabaret, set in 1930s Berlin.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Hello Dolly!: Trap: Louis Armstrong made it a hit in 1964, but it comes from Hello, Dolly!.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Let It Go: Trap: this one is from Disney's Frozen, not a Rodgers and Hammerstein show.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Somewhere: Trap: it is a tender song from West Side Story, with a lyric about a better place for lovers.
Songs from The Sound of Music.I Feel Pretty: Trap: Maria sings it in West Side Story, a different Maria from the nun.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Chim Chim Cher-ee: Trap: this is from Mary Poppins, a film that also starred Julie Andrews, which makes it a clever trap.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Feed the Birds: Trap: Walt Disney's favorite song of the Sherman brothers is from Mary Poppins, though Julie Andrews starred in both films.
Songs from The Sound of Music.Food Glorious Food: Trap: the orphans sing it in Oliver!, not The Sound of Music.

Famous music and opera venues.Carnegie Hall: New York's hall opened in 1891 with Tchaikovsky on the podium; a famous joke says that to get there, you practice.
Famous music and opera venues.Royal Albert Hall: London's domed hall hosts the BBC Proms each summer, and was built in memory of Prince Albert.
Famous music and opera venues.Sydney Opera House: Jørn Utzon's sail-roofed building, opened in 1973, is covered in over a million tiles, and he never returned to see it done.
Famous music and opera venues.La Scala: Milan's opera house opened in 1778 and staged premieres by Verdi and Puccini.
Famous music and opera venues.Hollywood Bowl: The giant outdoor amphitheater is home to the LA Philharmonic's summer season, and The Beatles played there in 1964.
Famous music and opera venues.Red Rocks: A natural amphitheater in Colorado between huge sandstone rocks, famous for U2's 1983 concert film Under a Blood Red Sky.
Famous music and opera venues.Metropolitan Opera: The largest opera company in the US, performing at Lincoln Center in New York.
Famous music and opera venues.Apollo Theater: A Harlem venue famous for Amateur Night, where Ella Fitzgerald won in 1934.
Famous music and opera venues.Grand Ole Opry: Nashville's country radio show has been running since 1925, with a stage made partly from the old Ryman Auditorium.
Famous music and opera venues.The Cavern Club: A Liverpool club where The Beatles played nearly 300 times.
Famous music and opera venues.Vienna State Opera: The Austrian capital's opera house opened in 1869, and each year is transformed for the Opera Ball.
Famous music and opera venues.Bolshoi Theatre: Moscow's big theater, where Swan Lake premiered in 1877; Bolshoi means big.
Famous music and opera venues.Abbey Road Studios: The London recording studio, made famous by the zebra crossing on the 1969 Beatles cover, is a place to record, not a venue to attend.
Famous music and opera venues.Sun Studio: The Memphis studio where Elvis and Johnny Cash recorded; it's a recording space, not a concert hall.
Famous music and opera venues.Graceland: Elvis Presley's Memphis home, now a museum, not a music venue.
Famous music and opera venues.Louvre: The Paris museum of art, home to the Mona Lisa, not a music venue.
Famous music and opera venues.Buckingham Palace: The royal residence in London; royal concerts happen there only on special occasions.
Famous music and opera venues.Walk of Fame: The Hollywood sidewalk with stars; it's a tribute, not a stage.
Famous music and opera venues.Big Ben: The famous bell, named Big Ben, is actually the bell inside Elizabeth Tower, not a concert venue.
Famous music and opera venues.Statue of Liberty: The statue was a gift from France, dedicated in 1886, and is a monument, not a stage.
Famous music and opera venues.Eiffel Tower: Finished in 1889, the Paris landmark was meant to be temporary.
Famous music and opera venues.Penny Lane: The Liverpool street in the Beatles song of the same name, not a venue.
Famous music and opera venues.Strawberry Fields: The name of a Liverpool Salvation Army home, remembered in a song, as well as a Central Park memorial for John Lennon.
Famous music and opera venues.Tate Modern: London's modern art museum in a former power station; its Turbine Hall hosts art, not opera.

Water sports.Surfing: It began with ancient Polynesians, and Duke Kahanamoku of Hawaii spread it worldwide; it joined the Olympics in 2020.
Water sports.Water polo: Players can't touch the pool bottom, so they stay afloat by 'eggbeater' kicking for four quarters; it's one of the oldest Olympic team sports.
Water sports.Rowing: Rowers face backward, so they can't see where they're going; a coxswain steers for the crew in some boats.
Water sports.Kayaking: The Inuit invented the kayak; its name means 'hunter's boat', and the originals were seal skin over a frame.
Water sports.Canoeing: Canoes date back thousands of years, and the oldest known one, the Pesse canoe, is about 10,000 years old.
Water sports.Sailing: Sailboats can go faster than the wind through clever angles, and America's Cup is the sport's oldest trophy, from 1851.
Water sports.Diving: Olympic divers hit the water at around 50 km/h from a 10 m platform, and the best barely splash.
Water sports.Water skiing: Invented in 1922 by Ralph Samuelson, who used barrel staves as skis on a lake in Minnesota.
Water sports.Kitesurfing: Riders are towed across water by a power kite, and can jump high; it became Olympic in 2024.
Water sports.Windsurfing: A mix of sailing and surfing, which was an Olympic sport in 1984, and can reach speeds beyond 50 mph.
Water sports.Wakeboarding: Evolved from water skiing and surfing, and riders use a boat's wake as a ramp to launch jumps.
Water sports.Rafting: Whitewater rapids are graded from class I to VI, where VI is considered extremely dangerous.
Water sports.Paddleboarding: The stand-up kind began with Hawaiian surf instructors, who used a paddle to watch their students.
Water sports.Curling: An ice sport, not water; the ice is sprayed with tiny droplets called pebble to create friction.
Water sports.Luge: A sled sport, where athletes lie on their backs, with speeds of up to 140 km/h on ice.
Water sports.Ice hockey: It's played on frozen water, but it's called an ice sport, not a water sport.
Water sports.Skeleton: Athletes dive headfirst down an ice track on a sled, reaching speeds like 130 km/h.
Water sports.Sandboarding: Done on desert dunes, with snowboard-like boards, so it's water-free.
Water sports.Snowboarding: Snow is frozen water, but the sport is considered a snow sport, not a water sport.
Water sports.Skateboarding: A land sport, which joined the Olympics in 2020.
Water sports.Bobsleigh: Sledding on ice, with a fast crew; it's a winter sport, not a water one.
Water sports.Fencing: A sword sport on a dry strip; its swords are electrically wired to score hits.
Water sports.Biathlon: Skiing and shooting over snow, so not a water sport.
Water sports.Pole vault: An athletics event on dry land, with no water in sight.

Greek Olympian gods.Zeus: King of the gods who ruled from Mount Olympus. His weapon was the thunderbolt, forged for him by the Cyclopes.
Greek Olympian gods.Hera: Queen of the gods and protector of marriage. Myths often show her taking revenge on Zeus's many lovers.
Greek Olympian gods.Poseidon: God of the sea, earthquakes and horses. He carried a trident and, in myth, lost a contest with Athena to be Athens's patron.
Greek Olympian gods.Athena: Goddess of wisdom and strategy, born fully armored from Zeus's head. Athens is named for her, and the Parthenon honored her.
Greek Olympian gods.Apollo: God of music, prophecy, healing and the sun. He presided over the oracle at Delphi, where visitors sought answers.
Greek Olympian gods.Artemis: Goddess of the hunt and the moon, twin of Apollo. Her temple at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders.
Greek Olympian gods.Ares: God of war, though the Greeks did not love him. Athena, who stood for strategy, was far more admired.
Greek Olympian gods.Aphrodite: Goddess of love and beauty, said to be born from sea foam. She was married to Hephaestus, the smith god.
Greek Olympian gods.Hermes: Messenger of the gods, with winged sandals. He also guided souls to the underworld and protected travelers and thieves.
Greek Olympian gods.Hephaestus: God of fire and the forge, and the craftsman of the gods. He was the only Olympian who was lame, in the myths.
Greek Olympian gods.Demeter: Goddess of the harvest. Her grief over her daughter Persephone was the Greek explanation for winter.
Greek Olympian gods.Dionysus: God of wine and theater, and the last god to join Olympus. Greek drama grew out of festivals held in his honor.
Greek Olympian gods.Jupiter: The Roman counterpart of Zeus. The name is Roman, so this is a trap: the gods here must be Greek.
Greek Olympian gods.Thor: The Norse god of thunder, wielding the hammer Mjolnir. He belongs to Scandinavian myth, not Greek.
Greek Olympian gods.Odin: The Norse chief god, who gave up an eye for wisdom. He rules from Asgard, not Mount Olympus, so he is a Norse figure here.
Greek Olympian gods.Ra: The Egyptian sun god, often shown with a falcon head and a sun disk. He is not a Greek deity.
Greek Olympian gods.Mars: The Roman war god, the counterpart of Ares. The planet Mars bears his name, but he is Roman rather than Greek.
Greek Olympian gods.Venus: The Roman goddess of love, the match for Aphrodite. Greek lists use the Greek name instead.
Greek Olympian gods.Neptune: The Roman sea god, matching Poseidon. The planet Neptune carries his name, but the Greek list calls the sea god Poseidon.
Greek Olympian gods.Anubis: The Egyptian jackal-headed god of embalming and the dead. He belongs to the Nile, not Olympus.
Greek Olympian gods.Loki: A Norse trickster who shapeshifts and stirs up trouble for the gods. He is Scandinavian, not Greek.
Greek Olympian gods.Freya: The Norse goddess of love, war and magic. Friday is named after her or after the goddess Frigg.
Greek Olympian gods.Osiris: The Egyptian god of the afterlife, killed and revived in myth. He is a Nile figure, not Greek.
Greek Olympian gods.Minerva: The Roman goddess of wisdom, the match of Athena. Her name is Latin, so it doesn't fit the Greek list.

Gods and goddesses of love.Aphrodite: Greek goddess of love, said to have risen from the sea foam near Cyprus. Her name may come from the Greek for "foam."
Gods and goddesses of love.Venus: The Roman goddess of love, who gave her name to Friday in the Romance languages, like French "vendredi."
Gods and goddesses of love.Eros: The Greek god of desire, who in later art became a mischievous winged child with a bow. His arrows made hearts fall.
Gods and goddesses of love.Cupid: The Roman counterpart of Eros, a winged archer. Valentine's Day pictures borrow him.
Gods and goddesses of love.Freya: A Norse goddess of love, beauty and also war. She drove a chariot pulled by cats, and wore a famous necklace, Brisingamen.
Gods and goddesses of love.Hathor: The Egyptian goddess of love, music and joy, often shown as a cow or with cow's horns. The Greeks equated her with Aphrodite.
Gods and goddesses of love.Ishtar: The Mesopotamian goddess of love and war, who was linked with the planet Venus. Babylon's grand Ishtar Gate was built for her.
Gods and goddesses of love.Kamadeva: The Hindu god of desire, who carries a bow of sugarcane with bees for a string. Shiva burned him to ash with a glance.
Gods and goddesses of love.Amor: Latin for "love," and a Roman name for Cupid. The word root gives Spanish "amor" and French "amour."
Gods and goddesses of love.Ares: The Greek war god. He was Aphrodite's lover, but he's not a god of love.
Gods and goddesses of love.Mars: The Roman war god, who loved Venus in myth, but the domain is war.
Gods and goddesses of love.Hades: God of the underworld, who kidnapped Persephone to make her his queen. Passion wasn't his role, so he is no love god.
Gods and goddesses of love.Thor: The Norse thunder god, married to golden-haired Sif. Love was never his department; Freya held that role.
Gods and goddesses of love.Athena: The goddess of wisdom, who stayed a virgin. Not tied to love.
Gods and goddesses of love.Hermes: The Greek messenger, who fathered Hermaphroditus with Aphrodite. He is a god of travel and trade, not love.
Gods and goddesses of love.Hephaestus: The Greek smith god, who was married to Aphrodite. He is a craftsman, not a love god.
Gods and goddesses of love.Vulcan: The Roman smith god and husband of Venus. He is a god of fire, not of love.
Gods and goddesses of love.Apollo: A god of music, sun and prophecy. He had many love affairs, but he isn't a love god.
