Gods and goddesses of love.Artemis: Greek huntress and goddess of the moon who rejected love and marriage.
Gods and goddesses of love.Anubis: The jackal-headed Egyptian god of embalming, not love.
Gods and goddesses of love.Poseidon: Greek lord of the sea and earthquakes, famously hot-tempered. Love wasn't his realm, despite many mythical affairs.
Gods and goddesses of love.Tyr: The Norse god of law, war and justice. He's tied to oaths, not love.
Gods and goddesses of love.Hel: The Norse ruler of the realm of the dead, said to be half living, half corpse in appearance. Nothing to do with love.
Gods and goddesses of love.Nemesis: The Greek goddess of retribution who punished arrogance. Her domain is revenge, not love.

Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Printing press: The technology was a century old; Shakespeare's plays were printed in small quartos, and the First Folio followed in 1623.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Telescope: The Dutch invented it in 1608, and Galileo's improved version in 1609 came while Shakespeare was still writing.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Globe Theatre: It opened in 1599 and burned down in 1613 when a cannon fired during Henry VIII set the thatch alight.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Tower of London: In his day it held prisoners and a royal menagerie that included lions, which Londoners paid to see.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Stonehenge: Already about 4,500 years old, it was a ruin; Inigo Jones studied it for King James I around his time.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Mona Lisa: Leonardo painted it in the early 1500s, about 60 years before Shakespeare was born, and it was not yet world famous.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Sistine Chapel: Michelangelo finished the ceiling in 1512, and he died in 1564, the same year Shakespeare was born.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Gunpowder: He lived through the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, when Guy Fawkes was caught with barrels under Parliament.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Pocket watch: Early portable watches, nicknamed Nuremberg eggs, appeared in the 1500s, though they were costly and not very accurate.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Eyeglasses: They were over 300 years old and common enough that Shakespeare's characters mention spectacles.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Mechanical clock: Towns had chimed with them since the 1300s; Shakespeare even put a striking clock into ancient Rome in Julius Caesar.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Steam engine: Newcomen's engine arrived in 1712, nearly a century after Shakespeare died, and Savery's pump came in 1698.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Pendulum clock: Huygens invented it in 1656, forty years after Shakespeare's death, so he told time by sundials and chimes.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Piano: Cristofori built the first around 1700, so Shakespeare's music was lutes and virginals.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Taj Mahal: Shah Jahan built it in the 1630s and 1640s, after Shakespeare had already died in 1616.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Big Ben: The tower and bell date from the 1850s, over 230 years after Shakespeare's death.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Light bulb: Edison and Swan made practical ones around 1879, so Shakespeare's London was lit by candles and torches.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Railway: Steam railways came in the early 1800s; Shakespeare's London only had horse-drawn carts and boats on the Thames.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Barometer: Torricelli built it in 1643, 27 years after Shakespeare died, so his weather talk was folk wisdom.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Telephone: Bell's 1876 patent was 260 years after he died, so he relied on messengers and letters.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Bicycle: The first pedal-less bicycles came around 1817, about two centuries after Shakespeare's death.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Versailles palace: Louis XIV made it a grand palace from the 1660s on, long after Shakespeare died.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Buckingham Palace: It began as Buckingham House in 1703, almost a century after Shakespeare's death.
Existed in Shakespeare's lifetime.Isaac Newton: Born on Christmas Day 1642 by the old calendar, he arrived 26 years after Shakespeare died.

Things in a pencil case.Pencil: Pencil lead is actually graphite mixed with clay, and the hardness ratings like 2B or 4H come from that mix.
Things in a pencil case.Eraser: Before rubber erasers, people rubbed out pencil marks with bread, and rubber got its name in England for rubbing out marks.
Things in a pencil case.Sharpener: The pencil sharpener was patented in France in 1847 by Bernard Lassimonne, and the small versions are still in use.
Things in a pencil case.Pen: The ballpoint pen was patented in 1888 but became practical in the 1930s after Laszlo Biro refined it.
Things in a pencil case.Highlighter: The first modern highlighter, the Hi-Liter, appeared in 1963, and its ink is a translucent fluorescent dye.
Things in a pencil case.Glue stick: The glue stick was invented in Germany in the late 1960s by Henkel, inspired by a lipstick tube.
Things in a pencil case.Protractor: A protractor measures angles in degrees, and a full circle is 360 because ancient Babylonians counted in base 60.
Things in a pencil case.Compass: A school compass draws circles by fixing one point and swinging a pencil around it, a technique that dates to ancient Greece.
Things in a pencil case.Crayons: The name Crayola blends the French craie for chalk and ola for oily, and the company has made over 100 colors.
Things in a pencil case.Felt-tip pen: The felt-tip was invented in Japan in the early 1960s, and its porous tip draws ink by capillary action.
Things in a pencil case.Short ruler: A short ruler fits in the case, and is just 15 cm or 6 inches, while a classic school one is typically 30 cm.
Things in a pencil case.Fineliner: A fineliner has a very thin plastic tip that makes steady, narrow lines, which is why it is popular for drawing and notes.
Things in a pencil case.Textbook: A textbook is too large and heavy for a pencil case, though it holds the facts the pencils are used to note down.
Things in a pencil case.Lunchbox: It holds lunch and is far too big. The metal lunchbox with TV characters took off in 1950.
Things in a pencil case.Water bottle: Too large for a case and a poor neighbor for paper. Water bottles hold liquid and usually ride in the backpack.
Things in a pencil case.Backpack: The backpack holds the case, not the other way around. Modern ones rest weight on the hips to ease strain.
Things in a pencil case.Laptop: Laptops would never fit in a pencil case, and the first portable computers weighed more than a bag of sugar.
Things in a pencil case.Hole punch: Usually too big and kept on a desk, though a mini one can fit. Most use the standard of two holes 80 mm apart.
Things in a pencil case.Desk lamp: It stays on the desk and needs a cord or battery. Adjustable-arm lamps like the Anglepoise date to the 1930s.
Things in a pencil case.Globe: A globe stays on a shelf or desk. The oldest surviving globe dates to around 1492.
Things in a pencil case.Whiteboard: Much too big for a pencil case. Whiteboards replaced chalkboards in many places because they are dust free.
Things in a pencil case.Chair: It is furniture for sitting, far too big for a pencil case.
Things in a pencil case.Paper shredder: An office machine, too big for a pencil case. The shredder was invented in 1909 by Abbot Augustus Low.
Things in a pencil case.Filing cabinet: Large office furniture, not a pencil-case item. Filing cabinets became common in offices around the 1890s.

Things with a zipper.Backpack: Many packs use two sliders on one zipper track, so you can open the bag from either end and padlock the pulls together.
Things with a zipper.Suitcase: Zippers made suitcases expandable: that extra inch of packing room is a second zipper hiding in a fold around the case.
Things with a zipper.Tent: Tent zippers take a beating from grit and rain, so makers coat the fabric tape in waterproof layers and add storm flaps over the teeth.
Things with a zipper.Sleeping bag: Bag zippers snag on fabric constantly, which is why good ones have a stiff anti-snag strip running along the whole track.
Things with a zipper.Pencil case: The classic school pencil case is a zippered pouch, often with a tiny pull tab that outlives the pencils inside it.
Things with a zipper.Duffel bag: The duffel is named for Duffel, a Belgian town known for the thick woolen cloth once used to make these bags.
Things with a zipper.Jeans: Levi's riveted jeans were button-fly originals; zip flies took over in the mid-1900s and button flies stayed the choice for purists.
Things with a zipper.Windbreaker: A full-length front zip lets you seal out wind in a second, and many windbreakers pack down into their own pocket.
Things with a zipper.Garment bag: The long zipper on a garment bag opens nearly its whole length so a suit can hang flat instead of being folded.
Things with a zipper.Fleece jacket: Fleece was invented in 1979 by Malden Mills, which never patented it, so the soft synthetic spread to every outdoor brand.
Things with a zipper.T-shirt: A pullover has no fastener at all: the neck hole is cut wide enough to stretch over your head, and that stretchy knit does all the work.
Things with a zipper.Sock: Socks have no zipper because knit fabric stretches to fit; a zip would only add a hard edge against your foot.
Things with a zipper.Necktie: The necktie is tied, not zipped, though clip-on and pre-tied versions with hooks exist for people who dodge the knot.
Things with a zipper.Scarf: A scarf stays on by wrapping or knotting, which is why no one has needed to add a zipper to a plain strip of cloth.
Things with a zipper.Beanie: A knit beanie stretches over the head, so it needs no fastener; zippered ones exist only as novelty hats.
Things with a zipper.Towel: A towel is a flat loop-pile cloth with no openings, so there is nothing for a zipper to close.
Things with a zipper.Napkin: Napkins are plain squares of cloth or paper; folding them into swans and fans is the only fastening they ever get.
Things with a zipper.Belt: A belt closes with a buckle, which is far older than the zipper; buckles date back thousands of years.
Things with a zipper.Plate: Plates are rigid and open; the nearest thing to a closure is a lid, and that gets a different word entirely.
Things with a zipper.Mug: A mug is a solid vessel with a handle, and the only seal it needs is the lid on a travel version.
Things with a zipper.Book: Books close with a spine and covers, no fastener needed; some diaries add a strap or a tiny lock instead.
Things with a zipper.Mitten: Mittens keep all four fingers together for warmth, and kids' ones often clip to a string rather than zip shut.
Things with a zipper.Bow tie: A bow tie fastens with a hook and slider at the back of the neck, which is closer to a buckle than a zipper.
Things with a zipper.Tank top: A tank top slips over your head with a plain neckline and no closure; zippers would add bulk to a light summer garment.

Household pests.Cockroach: Cockroaches can survive weeks without food and can hold their breath for about 40 minutes.
Household pests.Mouse: Mice can squeeze through a gap about the size of a pencil, which is how they enter homes.
Household pests.Rat: Rats breed fast, and a single pair can have dozens of offspring in a year.
Household pests.Ant: Ants leave scent trails, which is why a line of them appears in the kitchen after one scout finds crumbs.
Household pests.Termite: Termites eat wood from the inside out, and they cause billions of dollars in damage each year.
Household pests.Bedbug: Bedbugs hide in mattress seams and feed on blood, and they're hitchhikers in luggage.
Household pests.Silverfish: Silverfish are ancient insects that predate the dinosaurs, and they love damp books and paper.
Household pests.Clothes moth: Clothes moths, and not the adult, damage your wool, since their larvae are the ones that eat it.
Household pests.Flea: Fleas can jump over 100 times their body length, which is why pets pick them up so easily.
Household pests.Fruit fly: Fruit flies can appear from nowhere, because they're drawn to ripe fruit's smell.
Household pests.Dust mite: Dust mites are microscopic, feed on dead skin flakes and are a leading cause of indoor allergies.
Household pests.Woodworm: Woodworm are beetle larvae, and the little exit holes they leave are all you may see.
Household pests.Butterfly: Butterflies help pollinate plants and don't wreck houses, so they're welcome garden guests.
Household pests.Honeybee: Honeybees pollinate about a third of the food we eat and are protected in many places.
Household pests.Dragonfly: Dragonflies are ancient hunters that eat mosquitoes, so they help keep pests down.
Household pests.Goldfish: Goldfish are popular pets and can live for decades if well cared for.
Household pests.Hamster: Hamsters are kept as pets, and they stuff food in their cheek pouches.
Household pests.Parrot: Parrots are pets that can live to 50 or more, and some mimic human speech.
Household pests.Dolphin: Dolphins are wild marine mammals, and they have no business in a house.
Household pests.Owl: Owls hunt rodents, so a barn owl can eat thousands of mice in its lifetime, helping against pests.
Household pests.Penguin: Penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere and are not household animals.
Household pests.Earthworm: Earthworms improve soil, and Charles Darwin spent years studying how they do it.
Household pests.Koala: Koalas sleep up to 20 hours a day in eucalyptus trees, and they're no pest.
Household pests.Swan: Swans are protected birds in many places, and they live on lakes, not in the house.

Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Heart: Heart hides 'ear' in the middle, and it's the only organ in this list whose name holds a hidden body part.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Earlobe: The earlobe is the soft hanging bit of the ear, and it hides 'ear' at the start of the word.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Eardrum: The eardrum vibrates with sound waves, and its name starts with 'ear'.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Forearm: The forearm is the part between elbow and wrist, and it holds the radius and ulna bones.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Armpit: The armpit's name hides 'arm', and the medical term for it is the axilla.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Tear duct: A tear duct has 'ear' in the middle of 'tear'. It drains tears from the eye into the nose, which is why crying makes you sniffle.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Underarm: The underarm has 'arm' in it and it's another word for the armpit.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Inner ear: The inner ear contains the cochlea and the balance organs, and has 'ear' in the name.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Outer ear: The outer ear is the part you can see, which is made of cartilage and skin.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Middle ear: The middle ear holds the three tiny bones and is an air-filled space behind the eardrum.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Elbow: The elbow has no 'ear' or 'arm' hidden in it, even though it's part of the arm. Spelling matters here.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Knee: Knee has no 'ear' or 'arm' in its letters, so it doesn't fit.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Wrist: Wrist contains neither 'ear' nor 'arm'. It joins the hand to the forearm.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Shin: Shin lacks both 'ear' and 'arm', so it doesn't count.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Ankle: Ankle contains neither string, so it doesn't fit, though it connects foot and leg.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Chest: Chest has neither 'ear' nor 'arm' in its spelling.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Lung: Lung has no 'ear' or 'arm', though you'd need your lungs to say them aloud.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Eyelid: Eyelid has neither 'ear' nor 'arm' in its spelling, though it does contain 'eye' and 'lid'.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Palm: Palm has the letters P-A-L-M, so it never spells 'arm', even though it looks close. It's the center of the hand.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Hip: The hip is a body part, but its spelling holds neither 'ear' nor 'arm'. Spelling is the only test in this round.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Shoulder: Shoulder is part of the arm anatomically, but the word doesn't contain 'arm', so it's a trap.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Nostril: Nostril contains neither string, even though it is near the ear on the head.
Body parts with 'ear' or 'arm' in them.Thigh: Thigh contains neither string, and its bone is the femur.

Things that float.Rubber duck: In 1992 about 28,800 plastic toys, mostly ducks, spilled into the Pacific and floated around the world for years.
Things that float.Beach ball: A beach ball is mostly air, so it floats and drifts faster in the wind than you can swim after it.
Things that float.Cork: Most of cork's volume is trapped air sealed in tiny cells, which is why it floats so well.
Things that float.Ice cube: Water is unusual: ice is less dense than liquid water, so ice floats, letting lakes freeze from the top down.
Things that float.Pool noodle: Pool noodles are foam filled with tiny air bubbles, and crafters love them for projects too.
Things that float.Log: Logs float because wood is less dense than water, although some tropical woods like lignum vitae sink.
Things that float.Leaf: A leaf floats thanks to its thin shape and waxy surface, and surface tension helps hold it up.
Things that float.Life jacket: Life jackets use buoyant foam that keeps a person's head above water, even if unconscious.
Things that float.Feather: Feathers are light and trap air between their barbs, which helps waterbirds stay buoyant.
Things that float.Inflatable raft: An inflatable raft's air gives it enormous buoyancy for its weight, and some carry dozens of people.
Things that float.Coconut: Coconuts float, and they can drift thousands of kilometers and sprout on distant shores.
Things that float.Ping-pong ball: A ping-pong ball weighs just 2.7 grams and is hollow, so it floats even though it feels solid.
Things that float.Anchor: Anchors sink to grip the seabed, and the heavier they are, the better; some ship anchors weigh tonnes.
Things that float.Brick: A brick is denser than water so it sinks, yet a steel ship floats because its hollow shape displaces so much water.
Things that float.Cannonball: Iron cannonballs sink, and divers still find them around old shipwrecks.
Things that float.Coin: Coins sink, which is why people toss them into fountains and later fish them out for charity.
Things that float.Rock: Most rocks sink, but pumice, a volcanic rock full of gas bubbles, famously floats.
Things that float.Key: Metal keys are denser than water, so they sink, which is why floating key rings are sold for boaters.
Things that float.Hammer: A hammer's steel head is so dense it pulls the tool down, even though its wooden handle alone would float.
Things that float.Marble: Glass marbles sink; their density is about two and a half times that of water.
Things that float.Spoon: A metal spoon sinks, though a tiny light item can sit on the surface thanks to surface tension.
Things that float.Nail: Nails are iron or steel, nearly eight times as dense as water, so down they go.
Things that float.Wedding ring: Pure gold is about 19 times denser than water, which is why lost rings sink to the bottom.
Things that float.Dumbbell: A dumbbell is solid iron or steel, built to be heavy, so it sinks quickly.

Things that are triangle-shaped.Pizza slice: A pizza slice is a wedge, and New Yorkers fold it in half so the stiff crust holds the tip up.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Tortilla chip: Tortilla chips are often cut into triangles from a round tortilla, which makes sense since it gives no waste.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Yield sign: Yield signs are inverted triangles, the only road sign shape pointing down, chosen so it's easy to recognize.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Toblerone: Toblerone bars are formed into triangular peaks, a design inspired by the Matterhorn in the Swiss Alps.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Samosa: Samosas are folded triangles of pastry filled with spiced potato; they're a street food from South Asia and the Middle East.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Coat hanger: A coat hanger's triangular shape is stronger than a rectangle, as triangles hold their form under load.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Sail: A sail is often triangular, and the shape lets a boat sail at an angle into the wind.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Musical triangle: The musical triangle is a steel bar bent in a triangle with one open corner, so it rings when struck.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Shark fin: A shark's dorsal fin acts like a keel, and the classic triangle fin you see above the water is only part of it.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Pennant: Pennants are triangular flags, and in baseball, winning the league gets you the pennant.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Pool rack: A pool rack is a triangle that holds 15 balls in eight-ball, keeping them tightly packed for the break.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Coin: A coin is round, and its edges are often ridged or reeded, which started as a way to stop people shaving off precious metal.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Wheel: A wheel is a circle; it's one of the greatest inventions, yet it's not a triangle, which can't roll.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Dice: A die is a cube, with six square faces; it isn't triangular, though some game dice have 20 triangular faces.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Whole pizza: A whole pizza is round; a slice makes the triangle, which is the trick here.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Book: A book is a rectangle, not a triangle, and a standard book is about 1.5 times taller than wide.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Basketball: A basketball is a sphere, and has pebbled leather and seams, but no triangular corners.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Egg: An egg is an oval, and its shape lets it handle pressure from the ends, which is why it's hard to crush.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Door: A door is a rectangle, and the taller-than-wide shape is standard; triangle doors do exist only in A-frame cabins and tents.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Brick: A brick is a rectangular block; the standard size has stayed much the same for centuries.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Envelope: An envelope is a rectangle, though its flap is triangular, which is what makes the trap.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Phone: A phone is a rectangle with rounded corners; manufacturers say that's easier to hold and fit in pockets.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Donut: A donut is a ring, a torus, and its hole means it cooks evenly in hot oil.
Things that are triangle-shaped.Ring: A ring is a circle, which is the opposite of a triangle's angular form.

Things a beekeeper uses.Smoker: Smoke calms bees by masking their alarm pheromones, which makes it safer to open a hive.
Things a beekeeper uses.Veil: A veil protects the face and neck, which are the places bees tend to sting most.
Things a beekeeper uses.Hive tool: This flat metal tool pries apart frames that bees have glued shut with propolis, a sticky resin.
Things a beekeeper uses.Bee suit: White or light suits are standard because bees, whose natural enemies are dark-furred animals, tend to be calmer around light colors.
Things a beekeeper uses.Gloves: Gloves protect hands, though many experienced beekeepers work bare-handed for greater feel.
Things a beekeeper uses.Honey extractor: An extractor spins frames so the honey flies out by centrifugal force, leaving the wax comb intact for reuse.
Things a beekeeper uses.Frames: Frames are the wooden rectangles in a hive where bees build comb, and they can be lifted out without destroying it.
Things a beekeeper uses.Queen excluder: A mesh sheet that lets workers through but not the larger queen, keeping her eggs out of the honey.
Things a beekeeper uses.Bee brush: A soft brush gently sweeps bees off a frame so they aren't crushed when it is moved.
Things a beekeeper uses.Uncapping knife: Bees seal full honeycomb cells with a wax cap, and this heated knife slices it off before extraction.
Things a beekeeper uses.Butterfly net: A net catches butterflies for study, but a beekeeper works with the bees in the hive.
Things a beekeeper uses.Fly swatter: Swatting would anger the colony, and a good beekeeper moves gently.
Things a beekeeper uses.Bug spray: Bug sprays can harm bees, and a beekeeper protects them instead.
Things a beekeeper uses.Fishing net: A fishing net is for fish, though a swarm of bees can be caught with something similar.
Things a beekeeper uses.Lasso: A lasso is for cattle, and not for catching bees.
Things a beekeeper uses.Pitchfork: A pitchfork is for hay, so it belongs on a farm rather than at the hive.
Things a beekeeper uses.Saddle: A saddle is for horses, so it's not for the apiary.
Things a beekeeper uses.Scalpel: A scalpel is for surgery, and a beekeeper uses a hive tool.
Things a beekeeper uses.Ant trap: Ant traps protect homes, though ants can be a hive pest too, so a beekeeper may use different measures.
Things a beekeeper uses.Mousetrap: Mousetraps catch pests, but a beekeeper puts a mouse guard on the hive entrance in winter instead.
Things a beekeeper uses.Birdcage: A birdcage is for keeping birds, so it has no use at a hive.
Things a beekeeper uses.Spurs: Spurs are for riding, and a beekeeper's boots are plain.
Things a beekeeper uses.Harpoon: A harpoon is for whales and big fish, and not for honeybees.
Things a beekeeper uses.Fishing rod: A fishing rod is for fish, and a beekeeper works with hives.

Jobs ending in '-ess'.Waitress: Waitress is the female form of waiter, and modern restaurants mostly use the neutral server, but tips can be a large part of earnings.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Actress: Many awards, like the Oscars, still have separate best actress categories, though many performers now say actor for everyone.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Hostess: A hostess welcomes diners to a table, and the word shares its Latin root with hospital and hotel: hospes, meaning host or guest.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Stewardess: Stewardess was long the flying job title, with the first airline stewardess, Ellen Church, hired in 1930, who was also a nurse.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Seamstress: A seamstress sews clothes, and the word has the old -stress ending, from Old English seamestre.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Governess: A governess taught children at home, a job central to novels like Jane Eyre and The Turn of the Screw.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Priestess: Priestesses served in ancient temples, such as the Vestal Virgins of Rome, who kept the sacred fire for around a thousand years.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Abbess: An abbess is the head of an abbey of nuns, and medieval abbesses like Hildegard of Bingen wielded great influence.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Songstress: Songstress is an old-fashioned word for a woman singer, and the -stress ending is nearly dead in modern English.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Laundress: Laundresses washed clothes by hand, and in the 1800s it was one of the commonest jobs for women.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Lioness: A lioness does most of a lion pride's hunting, but lioness is an animal, not a job.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Tigress: A tigress is a female tiger, and the word is an animal, not a job, though it ends in -ess.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Mattress: Mattress comes from the Arabic matrah, meaning a place where something is thrown, and has nothing to do with -ess meaning female.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Fortress: Fortress comes from Latin fortis, strong, so its -ess isn't a female ending, and it's a building.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Address: Address ends in ess but isn't a job, and has the same root as direct.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Progress: Progress is a noun or verb, from Latin for to step forward, and not a person.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Dress: A dress is clothing, not a person, even though it ends in -ess.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Express: Express comes from Latin for pressed out, and is not a job.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Recess: Recess comes from Latin for to go back, and it ends in -ess, but it's a break from school, not a job.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Wilderness: Wilderness ends in -ness, a suffix for states of being, not the female -ess, so this is a look-alike trap, not a job.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Access: Access is a word with the -ess ending that has nothing to do with a job.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Compass: Compass ends in -ass, not -ess, and is a navigation tool. A hasty reader might think it fits, but it isn't a job.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Cypress: The cypress is a tree, and its name comes from Greek, a species not a person.
Jobs ending in '-ess'.Harness: Harness is horse gear or a safety strap, not a job title.

Plumbing parts.Pipe: Pipes carry water in and waste out, and are made of copper, plastic or steel in modern homes.
Plumbing parts.Valve: A valve controls the flow of water, from a simple tap to the hidden shutoff valve under a sink.
Plumbing parts.Faucet: A faucet is the visible end of the plumbing, and 'tap' is the British word for the same thing.
Plumbing parts.Drain: A drain carries water away, and needs a vent behind it so air can enter and water can flow freely.
Plumbing parts.P-trap: The curved P-trap under a sink holds a little water that blocks sewer gas from rising back into the room.
Plumbing parts.Elbow joint: An elbow joint bends a pipe, usually at 45 or 90 degrees, to turn corners in tight spaces.
Plumbing parts.Pipe coupling: A pipe coupling joins two straight pipes into a single longer run, and is one of the simplest fittings.
Plumbing parts.Float valve: A float valve in a toilet tank rises with the water and shuts the inflow when the tank is full.
Plumbing parts.Shutoff valve: A shutoff valve lets you cut water to one fixture so you can repair it without turning off the whole house.
Plumbing parts.Water heater: A water heater stores hot water in an insulated tank, with a magnesium or aluminum rod that is a sacrifice for rust.
Plumbing parts.Sump pump: A sump pump sits in a basement pit and pushes groundwater out so the basement doesn't flood.
Plumbing parts.Septic tank: A septic tank treats household waste underground where no sewer line exists, and needs pumping out every few years.
Plumbing parts.Fuse: A fuse is electrical. It is designed to melt and break the circuit when current gets too high.
Plumbing parts.Circuit breaker: A circuit breaker is an electrical switch that trips when overloaded. It belongs to wiring, not pipes.
Plumbing parts.Outlet: An outlet delivers electricity, and nothing about it carries water, so it belongs on the wiring side.
Plumbing parts.Light switch: A light switch is electrical, but it's a trap because 'switch' also describes some kinds of valves.
Plumbing parts.Junction box: A junction box protects wire connections inside walls, in the way couplings protect pipe joints, but for electricity.
Plumbing parts.Dimmer: A dimmer controls how much power goes to a light, so it's an electrical part, not a plumbing one.
Plumbing parts.Fuse box: A fuse box holds an old home's fuses, the electrical equivalent of a modern breaker panel.
Plumbing parts.Extension cord: An extension cord carries power from an outlet to something far away, so it has no place among pipes.
Plumbing parts.Light bulb: A light bulb turns electricity into light, and has no connection to pipes, water or drains in the house.
Plumbing parts.Doorbell: A doorbell is a low-voltage electrical circuit, a wiring job rather than a plumber's task.
Plumbing parts.Smoke alarm: A smoke alarm is a safety device wired to the home's electrical system, not a plumbing part.
Plumbing parts.Wall socket: A wall socket supplies electricity. Water and sockets don't mix, which is why bathrooms use special ones.

Cryptocurrencies.Bitcoin: Launched in 2009 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto, it has a hard cap of 21 million coins, and in 2010 someone paid 10,000 of them for two pizzas.
Cryptocurrencies.Ethereum: Proposed by teenager Vitalik Buterin, it runs programmable smart contracts, and in 2022 it cut its energy use by roughly 99 percent by dropping mining.
Cryptocurrencies.Dogecoin: It began in 2013 as a joke built on the Shiba Inu 'doge' meme, yet it later reached a market value of tens of billions of dollars.
Cryptocurrencies.Litecoin: Created in 2011 by ex-Google engineer Charlie Lee, it was pitched as the 'silver to Bitcoin's gold' and confirms blocks about four times faster.
Cryptocurrencies.Solana: This blockchain is built for speed, handling thousands of transactions per second, though it has suffered several network outages along the way.
Cryptocurrencies.Cardano: Co-founded by Ethereum's Charles Hoskinson, it is named after the Italian polymath Gerolamo Cardano and its development leans heavily on peer-reviewed research.
Cryptocurrencies.Tether: The largest 'stablecoin', USDT is meant to stay worth one US dollar, and it often sees more daily trading than Bitcoin itself.
Cryptocurrencies.XRP: Born at Ripple Labs for fast bank-to-bank payments, it was ruled in 2023 not to be a security when sold to the public on exchanges.
Cryptocurrencies.Monero: Its transactions hide sender, receiver and amount by default, which is why many exchanges have dropped it and regulators view it warily.
Cryptocurrencies.Venmo: A trap: Venmo is a payment app that moves ordinary dollars between friends, with no blockchain or coin of its own. Owned by PayPal since 2013.
Cryptocurrencies.PayPal: It moves regular money rather than being a coin, though it did launch its own dollar stablecoin, PYUSD, in 2023. Co-founders included Elon Musk and Peter Thiel.
Cryptocurrencies.Zelle: Run by a consortium of US banks, Zelle sends ordinary dollars straight between bank accounts. It is a payment network, not a cryptocurrency.
Cryptocurrencies.Euro: A government currency, not a crypto coin. Introduced as cash in 2002, it is now used by over twenty EU countries.
Cryptocurrencies.Yen: Japan's national currency and one of the most traded in the world. Central-bank money like this is the very thing Bitcoin was designed to sidestep.
Cryptocurrencies.Peso: The name dates to the Spanish 'piece of eight', whose coins were so widely used that they helped shape the first US dollar. Government money, not crypto.
Cryptocurrencies.Rupee: The word comes from Sanskrit for 'silver coin'. It is the national currency in India and several other countries, issued by governments rather than code.
Cryptocurrencies.Visa: Visa is a payment network that carries card transactions in regular currency. Some crypto debit cards run on its rails, but it has no coin of its own.
Cryptocurrencies.Mastercard: Like Visa, it moves ordinary money between banks and shops. It does partner with crypto firms for cards, but it is not a cryptocurrency.
Cryptocurrencies.Cash App: Block's app lets users buy Bitcoin, which makes it tempting here, yet Cash App itself is a payment service rather than a coin.
Cryptocurrencies.Apple Pay: It makes tap-to-pay purchases with cards stored on your phone. It never lets you pay in Bitcoin, because it is a wallet app, not a currency.
Cryptocurrencies.Stripe: Founded by Irish brothers Patrick and John Collison, it processes online payments for millions of sites. It has dabbled in crypto but is no coin.
Cryptocurrencies.Robux: Roblox's in-game currency is real money in a sense, bought with dollars, but it lives on a company server and can't be traded like crypto.
Cryptocurrencies.V-Bucks: Fortnite's in-game currency buys outfits and dances. It is a closed, company-controlled currency, so unlike crypto it can't be traded or sent elsewhere.
Cryptocurrencies.Klarna: This Swedish firm lets shoppers split purchases into installments. It's a buy-now-pay-later lender, not a currency, though it has flirted with crypto.

European tech companies.Spotify: The Swedish streaming service was launched in 2006 and its name is thought to be a mishearing of a shout.
European tech companies.Nokia: Finland's Nokia began as a pulp mill in 1865 and once made rubber boots before becoming a phone giant.
European tech companies.Ericsson: Swedish telecom giant founded in 1876 and still makes much of the equipment behind mobile networks.
European tech companies.SAP: Germany's SAP, founded in 1972 by former IBM employees, makes business software.
European tech companies.Siemens: Siemens was founded in Berlin in 1847 and started by building telegraph equipment.
European tech companies.Philips: Dutch Philips began in 1891 making light bulbs and helped invent the compact cassette and, with Sony, the CD.
European tech companies.ASML: Dutch ASML is the sole maker of the extreme ultraviolet machines needed to make the most advanced chips.
European tech companies.Rovio: The Finnish studio behind Angry Birds, released as its reported 52nd game after a long struggle.
European tech companies.Supercell: The Finnish company behind Clash of Clans which is a leading maker of mobile games.
European tech companies.Klarna: A Swedish payments firm known for buy-now-pay-later.
European tech companies.Arm: Cambridge-based Arm designs the chip architecture found in almost every smartphone, but doesn't make chips itself.
European tech companies.Ubisoft: The French publisher behind Assassin's Creed was founded in 1986 by the Guillemot brothers.
European tech companies.Logitech: Founded in 1981 by Swiss and Italian engineers, it's known for computer mice and webcams.
European tech companies.Samsung: Samsung is South Korean, founded in 1938 as a trading company, so it is not one of Europe's tech firms.
European tech companies.Sony: Sony is Japanese, founded in Tokyo in 1946; it co-developed the compact disc with European firm Philips.
European tech companies.Apple: Apple is Californian, born in 1976 in a family garage near Cupertino, so it is not a European firm.
European tech companies.Google: Google was started in 1998 by two Stanford students in California, which makes it American, not European.
European tech companies.Huawei: Huawei is Chinese, founded in 1987 in Shenzhen, and is a rival to the European network makers Nokia and Ericsson.
European tech companies.Netflix: Netflix began in California in 1997 as a DVD-by-mail rental service, so it is American despite its many European shows.
European tech companies.Nintendo: Nintendo is Japanese, founded in Kyoto in 1889 to make playing cards, so it is not a European company.
European tech companies.Intel: Intel is American and its name is short for 'Integrated Electronics'; it buys machines from Europe's ASML, though.
European tech companies.Dell: Dell was founded in 1984 in a University of Texas dorm room by Michael Dell, so it is American.
European tech companies.Lenovo: Lenovo is Chinese, even though it bought IBM's PC division in 2005, so it is not European.
European tech companies.Uber: Uber started in San Francisco in 2009 and is American, though it has large European operations.

Surrealist artists.Salvador Dalí: The melting clocks of The Persistence of Memory made him the best-known Surrealist, and he cultivated a famously flamboyant mustache.
Surrealist artists.René Magritte: The Belgian painter of The Treachery of Images wrote 'This is not a pipe' under a pipe, to show that a picture is not the object.
Surrealist artists.Max Ernst: A Dada pioneer who became a Surrealist, he invented frottage, rubbing pencil over textured surfaces to create dreamlike images.
Surrealist artists.Joan Miró: Spanish artist whose playful floating shapes and stars helped define Surrealism, he also designed the logo for a Spanish lottery.
Surrealist artists.Man Ray: An American photographer in the Surrealist circle, he made 'rayographs', photos created by placing objects directly on paper.
Surrealist artists.Yves Tanguy: Famed for desolate, dreamlike landscapes of strange shapes, he began painting after seeing a de Chirico work from a passing train.
Surrealist artists.Leonora Carrington: A British-born artist who settled in Mexico, she wrote the surreal novel The Hearing Trumpet and painted fantastical, witchy scenes.
Surrealist artists.Dorothea Tanning: She painted eerie childhood visions and later married Max Ernst; she lived to be 101, making art and writing poetry.
Surrealist artists.Meret Oppenheim: Her 1936 fur-lined teacup, Object, became one of the most famous Surrealist works and made her an overnight sensation.
Surrealist artists.Paul Delvaux: A Belgian who painted dreamy nudes in empty train stations and classical ruins, he is among the best-known later Surrealists.
Surrealist artists.Claude Monet: Though Monet's name is synonymous with Impressionism, he painted light and water, not dreams; he is the movement's namesake leader.
Surrealist artists.Andy Warhol: The Pop Art master made soup cans and celebrity prints in the 1960s, and he famously predicted 15 minutes of fame for everyone.
Surrealist artists.Roy Lichtenstein: He turned comic-book panels, with Ben-Day dots, into Pop Art; he is not a Surrealist.
Surrealist artists.Jackson Pollock: This Abstract Expressionist, known for his drip technique, favored pure gesture instead of Surrealism's dream imagery.
Surrealist artists.Keith Haring: His chalky, upbeat figures and subway art made him a 1980s New York Pop and street-art icon, with nothing to do with Surrealism.
Surrealist artists.Georges Seurat: He invented Pointillism with tiny dots of color; he painted A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, but was no Surrealist.
Surrealist artists.Gustav Klimt: Austrian Symbolist and Art Nouveau star of The Kiss, famed for gold-leaf glitter; his work came decades before Surrealism's start.
Surrealist artists.Henri Matisse: Often grouped with Cubism and Fauvism, he is known for color and cut-outs rather than dream logic.
Surrealist artists.Edgar Degas: He painted ballerinas and race horses, and was linked to Impressionism, a movement that predated Surrealism by decades.
Surrealist artists.J. M. W. Turner: The British Romantic painted stormy seas and glowing skies in the early 1800s, a full century before Surrealism emerged.
Surrealist artists.Johannes Vermeer: A Dutch master of quiet interiors and light, working in the 1600s, he predated Surrealism by about 250 years.
Surrealist artists.Grant Wood: The painter of American Gothic was a Regionalist, depicting the Midwest with stern realism, not dream imagery.
Surrealist artists.Edward Hopper: Painter of Nighthawks, he captured urban loneliness in realistic style; he's American Realist, not Surrealist.
Surrealist artists.Rembrandt: This Dutch Golden Age master of The Night Watch painted in the 1600s, long before Surrealism took hold.

Creatures found in Narnia.Faun: The first Narnia book began with Lewis's image of a faun with an umbrella and parcels in a snowy wood; he became Mr. Tumnus.
Creatures found in Narnia.Centaur: Narnian centaurs such as Glenstorm read the stars for prophecy and fight beside Aslan.
Creatures found in Narnia.Dryad: Tree spirits who wake from a long sleep in Prince Caspian and help drive out the Telmarines.
Creatures found in Narnia.Naiad: Naiads are water nymphs, and in Prince Caspian the river-god awakens to break the Telmarine bridge at Beruna.
Creatures found in Narnia.Minotaur: Lewis borrowed freely from Greek myth, and bull-headed minotaurs fight on both sides in Narnia.
Creatures found in Narnia.Satyr: Goat-legged woodland creatures from Greek myth, Narnian satyrs dance in Bacchus's revels.
Creatures found in Narnia.Dwarf: Narnian dwarfs vary from noble like Trumpkin to treacherous like Nikabrik, and fight on both sides of various wars.
Creatures found in Narnia.Giant: Narnian giants vary: some are stupid and fierce, and the giants of Harfang in The Silver Chair secretly plan to cook the visitors.
Creatures found in Narnia.Unicorn: Jewel the Unicorn is King Tirian's best friend in The Last Battle, one of many creatures able to talk in Narnia.
Creatures found in Narnia.Marsh-wiggle: The long-limbed, gloomy marsh-wiggles are a species Lewis invented, and Puddleglum is the most famous.
Creatures found in Narnia.Werewolf: Werewolves serve the White Witch among her monstrous army in the first Narnia book, and fall to Aslan's followers.
Creatures found in Narnia.Hobbit: Hobbits are Tolkien's creation in Middle-earth, and Lewis, Tolkien's friend, never put them in Narnia.
Creatures found in Narnia.Dementor: Dementors are the soul-sucking guards of Azkaban from Harry Potter, and Rowling has said they stand for depression.
Creatures found in Narnia.House-elf: Rowling's house-elves, such as Dobby, serve wizard families and are freed with clothes.
Creatures found in Narnia.Hippogriff: The hippogriff came from Ariosto's 1516 epic Orlando Furioso, before Harry Potter used it.
Creatures found in Narnia.Ent: Tolkien's tree-herding Ents belong to Middle-earth; Narnia has talking trees and dryads, but no Ents.
Creatures found in Narnia.Orc: Orcs are Tolkien's brutes, and the name comes from an Old English word, orc, for a demon.
Creatures found in Narnia.Balrog: The Balrog is the fire demon that Gandalf fights on the bridge in Moria in The Lord of the Rings.
Creatures found in Narnia.Oompa-Loompa: Dahl's chocolate factory workers were first written as African pygmies, and rewritten in later editions.
Creatures found in Narnia.Smurf: The Smurfs, tiny blue creatures, were created by the Belgian cartoonist Peyo in 1958, so they live nowhere near Narnia.
Creatures found in Narnia.Wookiee: Chewbacca is a Wookiee, a Star Wars creature, said to be inspired by Lucas's dog Indiana.
Creatures found in Narnia.Jabberwock: The Jabberwock is the beast of Lewis Carroll's nonsense poem in Through the Looking-Glass, not C. S. Lewis's Narnia.
Creatures found in Narnia.Thestral: Thestrals are winged horses in Harry Potter, visible only to those who have seen death, and not found in Narnia.
Creatures found in Narnia.Nazgûl: The nine Nazgûl are Tolkien's Ringwraiths, once kings of men, now servants of Sauron.

German vehicle brands.BMW: BMW stands for Bayerische Motoren Werke, and it began making aircraft engines; its blue-and-white logo echoes Bavaria's flag.
German vehicle brands.Audi: Audi's four rings stand for four companies that merged in 1932, and the name is Latin for listen, a translation of founder August Horch's surname.
German vehicle brands.Mercedes-Benz: The Mercedes name came from the daughter of an early dealer, Emil Jellinek, and Karl Benz built what's often called the first practical car in 1886.
German vehicle brands.Porsche: Porsche's 911 has been in production since the 1960s, and Ferdinand Porsche also designed the original Volkswagen Beetle.
German vehicle brands.Volkswagen: Volkswagen means people's car in German, and the Beetle became one of the best-selling cars ever, with over 21 million built.
German vehicle brands.Opel: Opel was founded by Adam Opel in 1862, starting with sewing machines, and it has been owned by General Motors and later Stellantis.
German vehicle brands.Maybach: Maybach built Zeppelin engines and luxury cars, and Mercedes revived the name for ultra-luxury models in 2002.
German vehicle brands.Trabant: The Trabant was East Germany's iconic car, with a body of a plastic-like material called Duroplast and a noisy two-stroke engine.
German vehicle brands.MAN: MAN makes trucks and buses, and the letters stand for Maschinenfabrik Augsburg-Nürnberg; it's part of the Traton group with Scania.
German vehicle brands.Skoda: Skoda is Czech, one of the world's oldest car makers, and it's now part of the Volkswagen Group.
German vehicle brands.Seat: Seat is Spanish, founded in 1950 as Sociedad Española de Automóviles de Turismo; it's now a Volkswagen subsidiary, based near Barcelona.
German vehicle brands.Volvo: Volvo is Swedish, and the name is Latin for I roll; it invented the three-point seat belt in 1959 and gave the patent away.
German vehicle brands.Saab: Saab is Swedish and began as an aircraft maker, the name standing for Svenska Aeroplan Aktiebolaget; its car arm ended in 2012.
German vehicle brands.Fiat: Fiat is Italian, short for Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino, and it was founded in Turin in 1899.
German vehicle brands.Renault: Renault is French, and it's one of the oldest car makers still running, founded in 1899 by three brothers.
German vehicle brands.Peugeot: Peugeot is French, and the family firm made salt and pepper mills and tools long before cars; its lion logo is older than its cars.
German vehicle brands.Citroën: Citroën is French, and founder André Citroën began with double-helical gears, which is why the logo shows two chevrons.
German vehicle brands.Ferrari: Ferrari is Italian, and its prancing horse emblem was borrowed from a World War I fighter pilot, Francesco Baracca.
German vehicle brands.Lada: Lada is Russian, and it's built on a Fiat design, with the Zhiguli based on the Fiat 124 in the 1970s.
German vehicle brands.Alfa Romeo: Alfa Romeo is Italian, and its badge shows the Milan cross and a serpent, a symbol of the Visconti family.
German vehicle brands.Ford: Ford is American, and Henry Ford's moving assembly line in 1913 cut Model T build time from about 12 hours to about 90 minutes.
German vehicle brands.Lancia: Lancia is Italian, and the maker pioneered the monocoque body and the V6 engine, while its Stratos dominated rallying in the 1970s.
German vehicle brands.Koenigsegg: Koenigsegg is Swedish, a small maker of hypercars founded by Christian von Koenigsegg in 1994 and based in Ängelholm.
German vehicle brands.Vauxhall: Vauxhall is British, named after a London district, though it's part of Stellantis and sells versions of Opel designs.

Vessels powered by sails.Sailboat: A sailboat can travel almost directly into the wind, up to about 45 degrees off, by zigzagging, because its sail acts like a wing.
Vessels powered by sails.Windsurfer: Windsurfing became an Olympic sport at the 1984 Los Angeles Games, and it remains on the program with newer foiling boards.
Vessels powered by sails.Galleon: Spanish Manila galleons crossed the Pacific for about 250 years, carrying Asian silk and silver between the Philippines and Mexico.
Vessels powered by sails.Clipper: The tea clipper Cutty Sark, launched in 1869, survives in dry dock in Greenwich, London, and was among the fastest sailing ships ever.
Vessels powered by sails.Schooner: The America's Cup is named for the schooner America, which won a race around the Isle of Wight in 1851.
Vessels powered by sails.Junk: Chinese junks use fully battened sails and watertight compartments in the hull, ideas Europeans borrowed centuries later.
Vessels powered by sails.Dhow: Arab dhows with triangular lateen sails sailed the Indian Ocean for centuries, riding the seasonal monsoon winds to trade.
Vessels powered by sails.Ketch: A ketch has two masts, with the shorter mizzen mast placed ahead of the rudder post, which separates it from a yawl.
Vessels powered by sails.Sloop: Sloops were popular with Caribbean pirates because they were fast and shallow enough to hide in coastal waters.
Vessels powered by sails.Land yacht: Land yachts are wheeled sail-powered vehicles, and a wind-driven record car reached over 200 km/h on a flat dry lakebed.
Vessels powered by sails.Caravel: Columbus's Niña and Pinta were caravels, small agile ships, while the Santa María was a larger carrack.
Vessels powered by sails.Windmill: A windmill has sails and uses wind, but it stays fixed in place, so it is not a vessel.
Vessels powered by sails.Speedboat: Speedboats use engines. Sails are not needed for the roaring speeds they reach.
Vessels powered by sails.Tugboat: A tugboat's engines are small but powerful for their size, and they push and pull giant ships into port.
Vessels powered by sails.Hovercraft: Hovercraft glide on a cushion of air, a design inventor Christopher Cockerell first tested with a tin cans and a vacuum cleaner.
Vessels powered by sails.Gondola: Hovercraft glide on a cushion of air. Inventor Christopher Cockerell first tested the idea with two tin cans and a blower.
Vessels powered by sails.Kayak: Kayaks are paddled, and the first ones were built by Arctic peoples from sealskin stretched on frames of driftwood.
Vessels powered by sails.Canoe: Canoes are paddled, and the oldest known one, found in the Netherlands, dates to about 8000 BCE.
Vessels powered by sails.Steamboat: Steamboats made rivers like the Mississippi a two-way highway, because boats no longer depended on wind or current.
Vessels powered by sails.Submarine: Submarines sail beneath the surface under engine or battery power, so sails would be useless.
Vessels powered by sails.Jet ski: Jet skis use an engine-driven water jet, so there is no sail involved.
Vessels powered by sails.Paddle steamer: Paddle steamers use steam engines to turn paddle wheels, not wind, so they fall under steam, not sail.
Vessels powered by sails.Narrowboat: Narrowboats were once pulled by horses along towpaths and now use engines, so sails are not needed for canals.
Vessels powered by sails.Pedalo: Pedalos are pedal-powered pleasure boats you see at seaside resorts, with legs doing all the work.

Places in a hospital.Emergency room: Emergency rooms sort patients by urgency, a system called triage, from the French for 'to sort', first used on battlefields.
Places in a hospital.Operating theatre: The name dates from when surgery was performed in tiered amphitheatres so students could watch from rows above.
Places in a hospital.Maternity ward: In 1840s Vienna, Ignaz Semmelweis showed that doctors washing their hands in chlorine solution sharply cut deaths of new mothers.
Places in a hospital.ICU: Intensive care units grew out of the 1952 polio epidemic in Copenhagen, where staff pumped air by hand into patients' lungs.
Places in a hospital.Pharmacy: The word comes from the Greek 'pharmakon', which meant both remedy and poison, a good reminder of why doses matter.
Places in a hospital.Waiting room: 'Patient' comes from the Latin for 'one who suffers' or endures, so waiting here is, rather fittingly, in the name.
Places in a hospital.Radiology: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895, and one of his first images was of his wife's hand, wedding ring and all.
Places in a hospital.Morgue: The word first named a Paris building where unidentified bodies were displayed so the public could identify them.
Places in a hospital.Recovery room: Patients wake here under close watch because anesthesia can briefly affect breathing and blood pressure.
Places in a hospital.Outpatients: Outpatients go home the same day, and today most hospital care in wealthy countries involves no overnight stay.
Places in a hospital.Courtroom: Courtrooms hold trials, not treatment, though both have strict rules and robes of a sort.
Places in a hospital.Dugout: A dugout is a baseball team's sunken shelter beside the field, so it is a sports place, not a medical one.
Places in a hospital.Engine room: The engine room houses a ship's engines. It is a ship's heart, not a hospital's.
Places in a hospital.Cockpit: A cockpit is where pilots sit, and the word first named a pit for cockfights.
Places in a hospital.Bullpen: The bullpen is where baseball relievers warm up, and the origin of the name is disputed, but it is a sports place.
Places in a hospital.Throne room: A throne room is for monarchs, and no hospital offers one, whatever the waiting times.
Places in a hospital.Ballroom: A ballroom is for dancing, so it has nothing to do with medicine.
Places in a hospital.Dungeon: A dungeon is a prison cell, a medieval word for the castle's strongest tower, 'donjon', so it isn't a hospital room.
Places in a hospital.Hayloft: A hayloft is a barn's upper floor for hay, not a hospital's.
Places in a hospital.Wine cellar: A wine cellar keeps bottles cool and still. Hospitals use cool rooms for medicines instead.
Places in a hospital.Pit lane: The pit lane is for Formula 1 teams changing tyres, not for hospital stops.
Places in a hospital.Penalty box: The penalty box is for hockey players who break rules, so it is a sports place.
Places in a hospital.Box office: The box office sells tickets for shows, and hospitals don't sell tickets.
Places in a hospital.Bridal suite: A bridal suite is for newlyweds in hotels, so no hospital has one.

Toys that spin.Spinning top: Spinning tops are among the oldest toys known; versions from ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt are over 4,000 years old.
Toys that spin.Yo-yo: Introduced to America by Pedro Flores in the 1920s, the toy was later sold to Duncan, whose name now means yo-yo to many.
Toys that spin.Fidget spinner: Patented by Catherine Hettinger in 1993, it only became a worldwide craze in 2017.
Toys that spin.Beyblade: The spinning battle tops first came out in Japan in 1999, and the name mixes beyblade from the word blade.
Toys that spin.Dreidel: Each side bears a Hebrew letter, and together they stand for a great miracle happened there.
Toys that spin.Pinwheel: Powered by wind, it was known in medieval times as a toy, and it still appears in countless garden decorations.
Toys that spin.Whirligig: This toy dates back to the Middle Ages, and the name also belongs to a beetle that whirls on pond surfaces.
Toys that spin.Gyroscope: Spinning wheels resist tilting, so this device is used in aircraft and spacecraft to hold direction.
Toys that spin.Frisbee: This flying disc began as pie tins thrown by students, and the name comes from the Frisbie Pie Company.
Toys that spin.Slinky: Invented by accident in 1943 when a naval engineer saw a spring fall off a shelf; it walks downstairs but never spins.
Toys that spin.Sticker book: Panini-style sticker albums turned collecting into a craze in the 1970s, but peeling and sticking involves no spinning.
Toys that spin.Pogo stick: Patented in the US by George Hansburg in 1919, it springs up and down rather than around.
Toys that spin.Rocking horse: Rocking horses took off in 17th-century England; they sway on curved runners and never turn in a circle.
Toys that spin.Teddy bear: Named for Teddy Roosevelt after a 1902 hunting trip where he refused to shoot a tethered bear; it stays put.
Toys that spin.Jack-in-the-box: It pops up when the lid opens, and the usual tune that plays is Pop Goes the Weasel, but it never spins.
Toys that spin.Etch A Sketch: André Cassagnes invented it in France, and Ohio Art sold it from 1960; the knobs turn but the screen only gets drawn on.
Toys that spin.Play-Doh: Sold first as a wallpaper cleaner, this dough is squeezed and molded, not spun.
Toys that spin.Lego: Its name is short for the Danish leg godt, play well, and bricks made in 1958 still fit with today's.
Toys that spin.Jigsaw puzzle: The first jigsaws were maps cut apart in 1760s London to teach geography, and the pieces lie flat.
Toys that spin.Rag doll: Cloth dolls are among the oldest toys; one was found in a Roman child's grave, and it does not move.
Toys that spin.Kazoo: Hum into it and a thin membrane buzzes, so it vibrates rather than spins.
Toys that spin.Stilts: Shepherds in France's Landes marshes once walked on stilts to see over the land, but they only stride.
Toys that spin.Building blocks: Wooden alphabet blocks were hugely popular in Victorian nurseries, and they only stack.
Toys that spin.Toy drum: You hit it with sticks, so it is a percussion toy that stays still.

Evil computers and AIs.HAL 9000: HAL 9000 turns on the crew of Discovery One in 2001: A Space Odyssey; the letters sit one step before IBM, a coincidence Clarke denied was intended.
Evil computers and AIs.Skynet: Skynet is the defense network that becomes self-aware and launches nuclear war in the Terminator films.
Evil computers and AIs.Ultron: Ultron is created by Tony Stark and Bruce Banner to protect Earth, and decides humanity itself is the threat.
Evil computers and AIs.GLaDOS: GLaDOS is the sarcastic AI of Portal, who promises cake and runs lethal tests on you.
Evil computers and AIs.Agent Smith: Agent Smith is a rogue program in The Matrix, played by Hugo Weaving, who multiplies like a virus.
Evil computers and AIs.SHODAN: SHODAN is the megalomaniacal AI of the game System Shock, and she considers humans insects.
Evil computers and AIs.VIKI: VIKI is the AI in I, Robot (2004) that reinterprets the Three Laws to take control of humanity.
Evil computers and AIs.AUTO: AUTO is the autopilot in WALL-E, who keeps humanity in space against orders, and is modeled on HAL.
Evil computers and AIs.Mother Brain: Mother Brain is the central computer in Metroid, and the final boss of the first game.
Evil computers and AIs.JARVIS: JARVIS is Tony Stark's loyal assistant, named after a butler, Edwin Jarvis, from the comics; he is a hero.
Evil computers and AIs.KITT: KITT is a heroic car; its red scanner light is shared by Cylons, but it is a helper, not an evil AI.
Evil computers and AIs.R2-D2: R2-D2 is no villain; the astromech has saved the heroes repeatedly, and his beeps were made by Ben Burtt.
Evil computers and AIs.WALL-E: WALL-E is no villain; he spends 700 years cleaning up Earth, collecting treasures like a Rubik's Cube.
Evil computers and AIs.Baymax: Baymax is no villain; the inflatable nurse in Big Hero 6 has a soft vinyl body and a mission of care.
Evil computers and AIs.Data: Data is no villain; the android in Star Trek: TNG studies humanity, but his brother Lore is the one who turns evil.
Evil computers and AIs.Vision: Vision is a hero; the android made in Age of Ultron from Ultron's body and JARVIS's mind fights alongside the Avengers.
Evil computers and AIs.Johnny 5: Johnny 5 is no villain; the military robot struck by lightning in Short Circuit refuses to kill because he's alive.
Evil computers and AIs.Optimus Prime: Optimus Prime is the heroic Autobot leader; he first appeared as a 1984 toy line and cartoon, and his motto is 'Freedom is the right of all sentient beings'.
Evil computers and AIs.K-9: K-9 is a robot dog, but a friendly one, from Doctor Who; the Doctor's loyal companion since 1977 isn't evil.
Evil computers and AIs.TARS: TARS is a loyal helper in Interstellar; he is a blocky robot with adjustable honesty and humor settings, not a villain.
Evil computers and AIs.Siri: Siri is Apple's helpful assistant, which debuted on the iPhone 4S in 2011, and it is no villain.
Evil computers and AIs.Alexa: Alexa is Amazon's assistant, which launched with the Echo in 2014, and it is no villain.
Evil computers and AIs.Robby the Robot: Robby the Robot is no villain; he is bound by Asimov-like laws and can make synthetic alcohol, in Forbidden Planet (1956).
Evil computers and AIs.Bumblebee: Bumblebee is an Autobot who befriends humans, so not evil; he often communicates using radio clips because his voice is damaged.
